articles.text:
SPECIAL TRADES INTELLIGENCE.

MR. ARCHIBALD Bum° s AND THE
MINERS.

MOST dour readers know that after a severe
atinggle between the Messrs. BRIGGS, and the
men working in their collieries in the neigh-
bourhood' of Methley and Whitwood in 1858, a
great step in advance was made for the future
peace and welfare of all concerned. Those
who take an interest in the progress of the
working people, as well as those who desire to
see the operations of capital carried on peace-
ably and profitably, were pleased to see in
this case of the Messrs. 'BRIGGS and their
colliers an arrangement of a co-operative cha-
motor carried out, whereby future peace and
friendliness between employers and employed
would be secured. •

It is needless to state hero the precise
arrangement entered into. It may be stated,
however, that it gave the men a power of
holding a certain portion of share capital in
the new company, and, under given conditions,
entitled them to share between them a pro-
portion of the profits as bonus on their wages.
Every man friendly to , co-operation looked
hopefully to this arrangement. It was the
first important attempt on the part of em-
ployers to introduce the co-Operative system
into their works, and according to all pub-
lished statements it answered admirably. It
was not what advocates of co-operation re-
garded as a true form of that idea, but it was
an approach so thoroughly in the right
direction, and appeared so well suited as a
practical first step in permanent reconcilement
between workmen and their employers, that
everybody who wishes well to both interests
was delighted with it, and prayed earnestly
for its success. Capital flowed into the con-
cern, an unusual prosperity began to manifest
itself, peace was secured, and altogether there
was reason to believe that capitalists generally
might be brought to see how much better this
new equitable arrangement Weis than the old
one, which led so frequently to strikes, lock.
outs, and all the strife and misery by which
they are usually accompanied.
It may be noted here that in seeking to
establish these new relationships the utmost
care should be taken not to excite old jealousies
and suspicions; not to alarm holders of
capital by straining the system unduly in the
direction of bonus:--a thing not much to he
feared; nor to excite the suspicions of working
men by any kind of hostility to their trades
unions, or anything else regarded by them a-
necessary for their Welfare, Indeed, in the
of the co-operative system, ill

whatever form, everything should be avoided
calculated to alarm the fears of the most timid
on any side, whether amongst the workers or
the capitalists.
In this view of the matter it is impossible
to condemn too strongly the conduct of Mr.
ARCHIBALD Bnloos, Managing Director of
the Whitwood and Methley Junction Collieries,
in relation to the colliers' demonstration which
took place at Leeds on Monday last. Every-
body knows that the colliers of the country
have, by means of their trade organization,
been obtaining considerable advantages in
regard to the price and other conditions of
their work, and, as is common enough amongst
working men (indeed amongst all classes of
men), they agreed to have a meeting for the
purpose of rejoicing in their success. Gene-
rally, speaking the employers of the district
acquiesced, and in some oases they even co-
operated by subscribing towards the expense
of banners and music. But not so Mr. Bnioas,
acting for his company. He who, if he
understood his position, ought to be pleased
above all others that the men were going
suceessfully on with that first step in organiza-
tion out of which the higher forms of co-
operation arc to come, took up an attitude of
angry hostility to the men which cannot fail
to seriously -discredit co-operation in their
eyes, and make it an object of suspicion and
dislike. Those who know better than Mr.
ARCHIBALD Bums what co-operation is, and
what it moans, should protest againt his conduct
in thus disparaging a great principle, in thus
begetting hatred for it in working men's
minds instead of respect; but his acts will go
further than their words, his angry tyrann y
will, instill the poison where there is little
chance of applying the antidote. Indeed it is
quite possible that by this foolish and most
unjustifiable act he may have sounded a war
note of defiant hostility between trades
unionists and co-operators, which will do more
mischief to the cause ef labour in one month
than he could repair during his whole life,
whatever its term, or however he might exert
himself to repair it.
To hold this great Leeds demonstration it
was necessary that the collieries of the district
should be closed on Monday, the 19th, and as
we have stated, that desire was generally
complied with by the employers. But, a 'few
days previous to the meeting Mr. ARCHIBALD
BRIGGS sent a printed notice to his men that
all their pits would be prepared for work on
the Monday, ,and that "every' man or boy
absenting himself will be coniidered to have
abandoned the co operative system, and will
thereby forfeit all claim to bonus on his future
earnings." It is difficult to see how a man or
boy can abandon a system by not being
present at a given spot at a stated time, and
it is more difficult still to see the justice of
cutting off' a man's bonus if Isis labour gives
him a claim to it—that is, presuming that the
system in which it is earned yields it by its
equity and not by the caprice of a manager.
But however this may be, the circular of
ARCHIBILD BRIGGS is a specimen of as naked
and disgraceful a tyranny as can well be
imagined in the present day.
To this circular Mr. JOHN DIXON, at the
request of the men, replied very modestly,
aud with singular moderation and temper.
He spoke of the Monday's pleasure trip being
known of for eight weeks ; of
,the •Whitwood
miners 'loins paid their money- in small

bonus cannot but regard themselves as

and, whatever justification may ba found in

such an act, looked at in the spirit of an honest

an oppression and a fraud.
But, whatever it may be, it certainly is not

and, if the threat thus so grossly held out

with Mr. ARCHIBALD BRIGGS and },liS anti.
unionist and anti manly pro- ccediugs.
By himself, and of himself, Mr. Bums has
a right to do as Ile thinks fit, or, by order of
his directors, be is fie to act as he thinks
proper, within the limits of his contract with
those for whom he acts; but he must not call
such conduct as be has indulged in in this
matter co-operation. We tell him it is not that;
it is not, in fad, in any one of its features
in the least like it. It is simply a mean tyranny,
sought to be worked out under the name, and
in the presumed interest, of co-operation. It
is the old habit seeking to assert itself in the
new circumstances, and those who are interested
in the new idea cannot but regard it with aver-
sion. When Ur. BRIGGS declares that the union
is working against his industrial partnership,
and that his men must choose between union
with his company, or union against it, he is

not antagonise co-operation. It is a prepara-
tion for it, and an advance towards it. It is

articles.title: PONTEFRACT ELECTION.
articles.text:
THE PONTEFRACT ELECTION.

THERE is one thing in the late Pontefract
election which is strange at first sight, namely,
the small number of voters who polled for
Mr. CHILDERS. It is easy to account for the
small number who polled for Lord ..POLLINOTON,
because, not only was that gentlonaan oue of
the feeblest possible specimens of the Tory
noblemen, but the most; damaging facts were
publi
'shed.bY Mr. CHILDERS as to his previouS
attempted political relations with the Liberal
11 party, which turned many of the Tory voters
away from him, and rendered his chance of
return quite infinitesimal. The TimqB of
Friday, however, not unnaturally, in its real
or feigned ignorance of the true circumstances
of the election, expresses considerable wonder
at the small number who voted for Mr.
CHILDERS (658 out of a constituency of 1,941),
and the small majority by which he, the
popular and intelligent candidate, who has
represented the borough for twelve years, was
returned over such an insignificant opponent
as Lord POLLINGTON. The reason, how-
ever, though ignored in the Times leading
article, will not be ignored by the Government,
and it is expressed by a correspondent in the
Times of Saturday, who professes to have
learnt the facts on the spot, and who says,
"Mr. CHILDERS was contending, not only with
the Conservatives, but with the Anti-Con-
tagious Diseases Acts Society; his loss from
this cause (allowing for Liberals who obtained
from voting, as well as from those who sup-
ported his opponent) was from 100 to 150
votes,"

As one who was present in 'Pontefract
during the contest, I fully endorse what I
believe to be the effect of this question intro-
ducing Mr, ,CHILDERS' majority, expressed in
the letter just quoted. Of course I am well
aware that any such estimate as that formed
above is open to 'question, and at any rate
it is difficult to establish its numerical
accuracy farther than by, saying that the
general consent of those connected with the
election seems to fix the number at about that
amount. We do, however, possess another
means of testing the effect of this question on
the election, of a kind quite as satisfactory as
if we possessed the exact numerical record of
the number of voters affected by it, for Mr.
CHILDERS obviously believed that he could
not secure his return without professing him-
self ready to vote for the repeal of the Acts,
and on every occasion he met the arguments
.
of the opponents of the Acts by declaring
that he was pledged to a Bill for
repeal, Which pretty well shows what Mr.
CHILDERS considered necessary to Secure his
return when we remember that it was he who
introduced into Parliament the Contagious
Diseases Act of 1866. The question may
fairly arise, then, in the minds of your readers,
"If. Mr. CHILDERS thus professed himself
about to vote for repeal, why was there any
further opposition to him,. and why . did the
100 to 160 electors above referred to still
abstain from supporting him ?." The answer
to that question is easy, for on further en-
quiry it appeared that the Repeal Bill which
Mr. CHILDERS said bel was pledged now to
vote for was not a simple Repeal Bill, but the
Government Bill introduced this session by
Mr. BRUCE, and withdrawn till a more con-
venient opportunity ; a Bill which, in fact,
while nominally repealing the Acts, really
extimds their i)rinciiile to the Whale nonnti3r.

—We must, remen3fier that there have been
already three Contagious Diseases Acts passed
in 186-1, 1866, and 1869, and that each re-
pealed, in whole or in part, the' one which
went before it, with the view of extending
the system of licensed prostitution Over a still
wider area. The repeal offered .by Mr.
BRUCE'S bill, for Which Mr. CHILDERS now
professes himself
.pledged to vote, is- of. this
nature,
,and perhaps I cannot better assure
your readers that'it is so that by referling to
the words used by Mr. BRUCE, who, when he
introduced it into the House of Commons, said
that though the meshes of the net were-larger,
he had given it a wider sweep, and that the
Bill would 4.‘ give. us. powers over the whole
country such ' as. We never • had before, and
reach places which could never be reaohed by
the present, Acts."

IBut, indeed, no reference beyond Mr.
CMILDERS himself is required to prove the
fundamental identity of this Bill, and of the
Acts themselves, for in his final speech on the
subject in Pontefract the evening before the
poll, while attempting to regain the confidence
of the electors by
,again reiterating that Mr.
BRUCE'S Bill was a Bill for repeal, he made a
strong speech in favour of the Acts and
in favour of that Bill in the same breath; and
it must be obvious to the meanest capacity
that if the' Bill in question really repealed the
Acts, it would be simple abiurdity in a man to
praise both. The eleotors of Pontefract, how-
ever, though doubtless partly galled by such
shuffling statements, were not altogether
blinded; and it will behove the electors of
other boroughs to watch that their repre-
sentatives who may be in favour of the
evil principle of these odious Acts do not
attempt to hood-wink them in a similar
manner. Mr. BRUCE, in reply to a deputation
of working men which waited on him the
other day on this question, said that the
majority of the Cabinet -were in favour of the
principle of these Aots. It is obvious, there-
fore, that when they profess to repeal thise
Acts, they ere incompetent to undertake at
the same time any constructive legislation on
this question calculated to satisfy the country.
When a Government, professedly in favour of
certain Acts, is forced, against its will, by the
voice of the nation to repeal them, the only
kind of repeal which it is capable of giving is
total and unconditional repeal, and a Bill
granting this is the only one which we can
accept at the hands of any body of men
wedded to the principle of the present Acts.
. JAMES STUART, M.A.
Fellow and Assistant Tutor of Trinity
College, Cambridge'.

articles.title: IMPROVIDENCE, LABOUR, AND LEISURE.
articles.text:
IMPROVIDENCE, LABOUR, AND
LEISURE.

UNDER the above heading the Scotsman has
taken the usual liberty of pitching into "the
working classes, or that portion of them under
trades union leaders, for conducting their
affairs quite irrespective of example, ex-

perience,:or reason."

This may not be proving much against them,
taking the usual ways of the world's ex-
perience as an example of reason; only the
Scotsman rates the workers for being fools
beyond even usual folly, because they are now
taking leisure when they can afford it, and
because they are doing, as their masters have
long done, restrioting their commodity as
they will, and selling it in the best markets.
To prove the case the Scotsman sets out with
quoting the proverb, "Make hay while the sun
shines ; "inferring, therefore, that the working
Glasses should double their product to meet
double demand. Instead of doing this, how-
ever, he charges them, i.e„ those under trades
union leaders, with" working less
,j ust because
they are better paid, and selling less, of their
commodity because they can sell it to greater
advantage." The srotsmitn gives us no proof
or evidence for his assertion, and we might be
content with simply denying his charge. But,
remembering the fact that all returns of pro-
duction show a very decided increase, we
turn the tables upon' the Scotsman, and charge
him with libelling, and falsely libelling, the
workers with producing less (under
,trades
unions leaders), and we challenge him to
prove in tho especial articles—coal and iron
ins,taneed—that " produotiun has diminished

AUG. 24, 1872.

because wages have risen, or that they work
less because of inoreased revenue."
Nothing can be made more misleading in
argument than analogy, and this misleading
is perfect in the use made of the old proverb
",make hay while the sun shines," as applied

to demand and supply in the ease of labour.
We might quote proverbs quite as good as
this, having another bearing, such as
"don't adi fuel to fire," "don't feed a fever,"
"don't over-work a willing horse," and
"don't put on the steam when going down a
steep hill:" and all these are quite as ar
plicable in argument, and certainly more
pertinent to the bearing of the vital question,
of the best course, than is that of the sun-
shine and the hay. The fact is, trade is not
sunshine, and speculation is not hay, and,
therefore, not the fade only, but the whole
conditions of the two cases are different. The
Scotsman knows this very well,. and, there-
fore, the fallacies and misleading involved
ought to be exposed. Hay so far as a product
of nature, and subject to seasons beyond the
control of man, must be made when the sun,
shines of course; and even then we must wait till
it is fully grown. But trade is not a product of
nature; it is an artificial arrangement of man',
for the provision of his necessities, or luxury;
and as such is tiot subject to the sunshine, nor
in fact, to any law of nature beyond his
control.

There are certain seasonal laws, such
as the provisions of clothing for summer and
winter, and of food in its season, &o. Bat
over years and seasons there is also a law of
uniformity as definite; but better known and
better arrangeable than are the seasons of
nature, or the conditions of natural production.
The fallacy consists in ignoring the well-
known tendency of selfishness, to set aside the
natural law of supply and demand, and to
speculate in trade, by supplying too muclrat

According to this's view, what are called by com-

All this was perfectly true then, and it is

remedied by regulating the supply. Regulat-
ing supply will, in the end, regulate demand

bringing up supply, to the extent of an
unnatural demand, can but come to loss, and,
must in the ultimate, end in ruin. 'Who, then;
are the wise nieti---;thoSe Who would stimulate,

The instincts of the people are often, though
they may not ktio* it, wiser really than the

the facts. It is to be regretted that some

"under trades union loadings." The pro-

and corruption alike, but of course these
take the benefit of prosperity, and abuse
it as they can. These are not the leaders
of trades unions, and they are its
pests. But how many and much of
these being so, are to be laid to the charge of
that School Of Scotsmen who Wetad let thinks
.alone to right themselves? "Each for himself,
and the evil, catch the hindmost," leaves its
leaven, as well as its victims. And these. are
the brutal, nay, coarse-minded, .who are made
So by ceaseless and unintelleetual toil,, from
whioh the rebound is a degraded sensualism
in the way of enjoyment.
None can regret the abuses thus arising
more than the true trades unionists; and
wherever these have had their—sway, they
have used their leading to industry, Sobriety,
and a wholesome measure of mental culture
and intellectual enjoyment. Witness . the
influence of, the Barnsley union executivn
upon the habits and morals of the coalminers
or South and West Yorkshire (whose pro-
duction was never equalled before); and of
the ironworkers' unions of Cleveland. These
men have been immensely, and therefore
undeniably, improved in every respect by the
leading of the unions. On the contrary, we
could a tale unfold of the vice, immorality,
and physical and moral depiavity, canied by
the unregulated over-work and under-pay,
of the unregulated competition, in flesh and
blood for wealth, before the introduction of
the Factory and Mining Acts. But we refrain,
for the present, asking the Scotsman merely
what be wants—men or wealth? And what
is wealth for, unless to be enjoyed.? That
the workers should enjoy themselves is a
grievous sin it some creeds; .and what is
astonishing (and yet it is not); these arc the
very people whose works lead men to the
evils they derogate, than to any good. That
principle of selfishness, which elevates itself
at the, expense of its neighbour, leads to
grumbling when disappointed; while it has
no remedy of its own for improvement. From
such Scotsmen we . may well pray, "Good
Lord deliver us."

JOLIN HOLMES.

IMPROVIDENCE-LA.DOUR AND LEISURE

(Front the Scotsman).

"Make bay while the sun shines," is an ad-
vice which has generally been regardatl as wise,
for the obvious reason that it is when the sun
shines that hay can be made both best and most
rapidly. But a large portion of the working
classes of this country appear to think that man-
kind have erred in believing in this and similar
proverbial advioes, recommendatory of making the
best of good opportunities. The sun is shining at
this time with unparalleled splendour upon nume-
rous departments of industry; but, in some .at
least of these departments, the working or wage-
reeeiving.elasses, getting at least their full share
of the sunshine, see in their good fortune a reason
rather for making less than more hay. In pro-
portion as the commodity they sell—i.e., labour
—fetches a better price, they resolve to sell the
less of it. The more sunshine, the less hay, is
their resolution—though they know, or at least
have experienced, the fact that, when the sun has
ceased to shine, they, will have to give more
labour for less pay. This would ho surprising—
rather it would be impossible—in any other class;
bat the working or wage receiving class, or that
portion of them under trades union leaders, are
apt to conduct their affairs quite irrespective of
example, experience, or reason.
It was not only proper and natural, but inevit-
able, that the late groat increase in the demand
for many_ of the products of labour should cause
a proportionate increase in wages, which are the
price of labour. But, strange as it may seem;
the result of an increased reward for industry
has, in certain employments—notably coal and
iron—been rather to reduce than stimulate
industry. Large masses of the working men are
preferring to take their prosperity out in ease or
idleness, rather than in profit. The increase in
the rate of pay is used to obtain, not an increale
of revenue, but a decrease of work. In some
'departments and districts; three or four days of
very few .hours each is held to bo enough of work
for a week, not because it is enough for the
strength, but because, under the increased rate of
wages, it is enough to subsist on. Now, it may
be desirable or natural that workmen should,
when they can afford it, buy some amount of
ease among the other luxuries which prosperity
puts within their reach. But they are buying
easier leisure too dear, by buying it at the wrong
time.

In all other classes and employments, the time
of high pay or profit is the time for increased not
reduced exertion. The lawyer does not begin
refusing bi iefs when higher fees are offered
'him; the merchant does not decline increased
transactions when profits rise-\; the manufacturer
does not set himself to produce, less when demand
and prices increase. What would he thought of
a mill-owner who, bev4uke the price el the um-

produdets had _doubled, resolved to,' re-
uce his preductions a half?, lie.weeld. simply,
be thotight Mad, and his nitiniato and earlybank-
riiptcy regarded as a eertainty, Yet this is -just
4hat certain sections of the 14bouring plusses are
doing at this moment.
,They are working less
because they are better paid—they are selling less
of their commodity because they can sell it -to
better advantage. By working more-4y,wOrlo•
in as much as they they did before and getting
mire money for that work than they' did
before—they would be able to. buy leisure
afterwards when leisnrehecoraes cheaper. •When
labour is dear, leisure, of course, is dear also,
for leisure is just a deduction from labour. For
the same reason, when labour is cheap, leisure. is
ohea.p. , The time will inevitably- .ccraet and come
goon, when labour and leisure will he both cheap'.
But when that time comes, the working men Will
no be able to buy leisure, cheap as it may. have
becqme, because their means .of buying it will
have been .proportionately redticed, and will, in
fact, have disappeared, for all their means will be
required for their bare subsistence. Labour is a
thing they sell—leisure is a thing they buy; but,
by their present policy, they are buying in the
dearest market, and, if not literally, yet virtually,
selling in the cheapest market, because, by with-
holding what they have to sell, they are making
no more profit out of a high than they did out of

they won't—hereafter will be; their time to buy,

BUILDERS' STRIKE.

A-LTI1.01:1011.1t is. often -of little use to offer
advice to men whose minds are. excited, yet
sometimes the still small voice of coinm,on
sense when appealed to may yet be heard.
The carpenters and joiners are to have a meet-
ing with the master builders with a view to
settle, if possible, their --differences. Now
'without entering on these poihts of difference,:
I beg leave respectfully to, suggest to, the men
that their contest is not that of a combat, but
merely that of a bargain.
In, a combat there is often a dislike to "give
in" on account of there being What is coUsidercd.
to be a certain amount of disgrace incurred by
so doing. And it is certain that in the battle-
field the degged valour which don't know

by victory. But in a "strike" the contest
is simply that of a bargain, and those who are
most celebrated as successful bargainers are
those who are quickest to perceive the tone of
the mallet, which indicates the price they
are likely to get, and to close with that price
accordingly; while those who 'outstay that
market, and are thereby unable to make ttfeir

jected to ridicule. Now it is always in

their eyes to the fact, to know when the

pected to be—to consider calmly whether the
remaining part of it, which will be determined
wholly by the economic question of "demand

their favour or not. My own *pinion lam
not called upon to declare. My object is to
place the question in its true light, that of a
bargain which 'it has now, more than ever,
assumed, and to remind the contending parties
that there can be no disgrace in accepting the
decision of the market, for. it is that which
must decide the question, whatever it may be.

IN this outline all that is true in the funda-
mental principles of ROBE= OWEN'S sYstem is
retained, but the errors wtich made his views
inexplicable and his plans impracticable, and
Which were the chief cause of the strong op-
position which they incurred, are corrected.
Aua in the place of these errors the truths
which were denied in them are added
to the truths which are the essential
part of this admirable combination of practical
knowledge upon subjects of the highest im-
portance to the human family. The chief of
the truths denied were the agency of man in
the formation of his character, and his power
gelf-ontrol, and, a fi a neceary idennee,

his moral responsibility (see A 2 and 3,. and B
in the preceding outline). The statement,
that "man's character, or , qualities, and his
opinions, feelings,. and determinations, are
formed for him and not by him," which is the ,
denial of our second_ truth, (outline, A 2), was
eenstantly substituted by Mr. OWEN for the
first truth (A. 1) and in addition to the denial ,
of man's floral responsibility, other exaggerated ,
inferences 'followed:, which,. being combined
with the , truths which follnw and
pideAlcally from the first :truth, the .funda-
Mental truth of,the system, imported a colour-
ing of errei and: exaggeration to other parts cf.
the 'subject. And. thus for a' tiine the succesii -
of the teaching of this most practical, and
seeing, anddevoted of philanthropists was made •
impossible. ROBERT OWN,] it should be
understood, was no more theorist, or man of
words, or of ordinary learning; .he was man
of great experience, who. had bad great oppor-
tunities for acquiring practicalknoWledgenpon
the most. important social subjects; and had
made excellent use of them. He had managtd
a working population of from 200016 !2,400
persons for many years, and. hiad- .ddndated '
their, children under the, guidance of his
knowledge of the Causes of evil and. of goo,l;
And although the favourable influences Which
he brought to bear were counteracted by
many highly unfavourable conditions., in local
prejudices and othoe circumstances, and in the
general circumstances of the present systoin, •
he had produced results, in improving Oily
character and.condition of the .adults, and
in forming the
.charaoter of the children, which
excited the astonishment and admiration of ,
thousands of persons, of all classes, -who ,
visited his .establishment a New,44anark.
And. at the same time he had directed with
great success the mattufaeturing and, commis...-
cid. proacedings ot his extonsi,vo Cotton thins,
and had rcalied. a considerable fortune.
The co-operative social system, therefore,
not the contrivance of a
,theorist, speculating
in his study; but it is a discovery which in
every , particular has
.beea ascertained and
, verified by extensive practice and, by careful ,
attentioL to facts, the only tests of truth.

The discoverer and founder of the new
system was meet successful while practically
applying his fundamental truth. But when
lie endeavoured to teach hi a views to the
World, success became impossible, as Stilted
abeveAnd dating his life, no one, 'among
the:Mende or the opponents of his views, was
able twoorrect the erroneous parts Of them,
and to separate the error from the truth. It.
was Mt, even by his disciples, that there was
something wrong or defective ia his teaching.
But the errors could not be finally removed,
and the missing truths could not be substituted
for them, while no one was able to analyse the
,mental operation by whioh we form determin-
ations and ex,ereise self-control, and to demOn.
stritte practically by doing so, that we halm
power to form ,determinations and power of
Self-oontrol.. This alone ,Could remove all
doubts upon the subject, and make. evident
the perfect consistency with each other of the
two truths (A: 1 and 2) which mast be known
before the causes of evil and of good in the
formation of character, Sce,, can be ascer-
tained. And the new system could never be
realised (bemuse the knowledge of these
causes, and the character of true enlighten-,
ment and enlightened goodness which are
necessary for its realisation, could never be
acquired), while the denial of the first truth
was combined with the assertion of the second,
as in the common idea of free-will, or while
, the denial of the second was combined with
the assertion of the first, as in the doctrine of
philosophical necessity, or while these two
supremely important truths were not under-
stood. Men and women who are ioznorant of
these truths, and of their practical application,
whatever other knowledge they -shay possess,
and however good their intentions may be,
cannot have the knowledge anti the character
which alone can enable them to construct and
carry out a satisfactory system of geoid co-
operation. With this knowledge, and with
the improved social feelings which. it will
produce, in those who have not been too much
deteriorated through the influences Of the
present system, the economics of the new
system, and the COlllitructivst of the zsw

arrangements, and the education of every I
fairly organized child to acquire a character
of true enlightenment and enlightened good-
ness, will be easy matters .of business—or
rather they will be highly pleasurable employ-
ments and amusements. And we may be
certain that when the means are known by
which the moral and physical evils of the
present system may be removed, the popula-
tion will not allow the system to be perpetuated
of which these evils are the natural and in-
evitable effects. How long shall poverty and
the fear of poverty be allowed to prevail as
they do now, and selfishness, and disunion,
and quarrels, and crimes, and miseries of every
possible kind, when the means arc known by
which in a comparatively short period they
may be made to cease I'
To state comprehensively the combination
of conditions which will constitute the New
Social System, I have arranged them in the
form of a "Sable. There are three divisions of
them—the ultimate, the primary, and the
intermediate.
The Ultimate Conditions are the Results to
be realised in each Establishment or Village
—the object in view being to form, for the
equal benefit of all, a combination of Causes
of Good, and by so doing to exclude, as far
as possible; the Causes of Evil.
The Primary Conditions are the first or
fundamental requirements which are necessary
for the realising of these Results.
The Intermediate Conditions are the Insti-
tutions and General Practices which will be
necessary for the application of the Primary
Requirements and the realisation of the Ulti-
mate Results.

-On considering this Table it will be seen
how opposite all these conditions are to those
of the existing system. They are conditions
of Enlightenment and Enlightened Goodness;
the conditions of the present system are cir-
cumstances of ignorance and. selfishness, the
natural consequences of tho defective intel-
lectual and moral character hitherto universal.
While men are ignorant of the causes of Evil
and of Good, and while they retain the defec-
tive moral development consequent upon this
ignorance, they can only form such social con-
ditions as those which have existed during the
past, and which now exist. When they have
acquired the Knowledge of these Causes, and
the improved or renovated character which
will be the natural effect of the influence of
this Knowledge upon the higher attributes of
man's nature, they will form the now combi-
nation of external Causes of Good as naturally
and inevitably as in their previous state they
have formed the combination of Causes of
Evil by which societies have surrounded
themselves in all the varied. forms in which
they have hitherto existed. All schemes of
Social Reform, therefore, in which it is pro-
posed to reconstruct the outward conditions of
Societies upon any other basis than the know;
ledge of the principles stated in the preceding
outline, are destitute of the foundation upon
which alone a system of Effectual Social
Reform can be constructed.

The combination of conditions presented in
the tabular statement could not have been
devised except under the guidance of the
knowledge of these principles and under the
influence of the improved social feelings con-
sepunt upon this knowledge. Nor could it
be realised practically by any society not
regulated in its proceedings by this knowledge
and these feelings, if an attempt were made
to do iso. Although the well-being and happi-
ness of man are in a very great degree
dependent upon external conditions, they can
never be realised by means of influences from
without unless the internal conditions exist
also which are the fundamental parts of the
causes of good. (See C 3 in the Oatline, and
the Special rtinutfy Conditions in the Table.)
All attempts, therefore, to attain a prosperous
and happy state of society in the absence of
the Eslentia/ Primary Requirements, must, of
necessity, be very far front satisfactory in
their results. And all mere material success,
if it could be realised, could give but a very
limited degree of happiness to societies while
they remained ignorant of the Causes of Evil
and of Good, and while they retained the
character which alone men can have who are
thus ignorant. The Social Reformer, there-

fore, who desires to understand the object of
his aspirations must study the preceding Out-
line with close attention until he has
thoroughly mastered every part of it.
In the Outline and the Tabular Statement
we have the leading points of a New Social
Religion, which may be adopted by men of
every theological creed, and which will enable
and cause those who adopt it to "love one
another," although for a time they may differ
upon points of theology. When men have
acquired the knowledge of the Causes of Evil
and of Good they will no longer allow their
theological opinions to excite them to mutual
ill-will and animosity. And they will modify
their opinions, so far as it may be necessary to
do so, to bring them into harmony with their
now knowledge. While they do not possess
this knowledge their religious opinions must
of necessity be deficient upon points of the
1 highest practical importance, and their
religious feelings must be deficient in like
manner.

For the present I must refer the reader, for
details, to my little pamphlet on "The Co-
operative System of Society," and for expla-
nations of the fundamental Truths (A. 1,2,
and 3), to my little work on "..Freo Will
and Law," published by Messrs. Longmans
and Co.

lIENEX TRAVIS.

PRESERVED FOODS.

On Monday, at the meeting of the British
Association, at Brighton, Dr. Edward Smith
read an instructive paper on "The Economic
and Nutritive Value of the principal Preserved
Foods: Preserved Milk, Preserved Meat, and
Liebig's Extract." He was not commenda-
tory to the milk-preservers, who are, he
thinks, doing much better for themselves than
for the public. The rationale of their opera-
tion is to reduce the bulk of milk by about
75 per cent.—that is, to convert four pints
into one. The pound tins, soli at from Bid.
to 10d., contain 14 oz. of pure milk and 2 oz.
of sugar, the total weight of the contents
being 4 oz. short of a pint. In its natural
state the milk would be worth from 21d. to
(lid., according to locality. Where, as in some
brands, the weight of sugar was increased,
there was a proportionate decrease of nutri-
tion. lie had heard that though the Ayles-
bury milk contained 2 oz. of sugar or 1.21 per
cent. ,'other preservers put in as much as 3 oz.,
or 20 per cent. It was a significant fact that
the preserving factories had all cheese-making
establishments connected with them. The
Americans acknowledge that a mixture of
new and skim milk make the most sale-
able compound. What the consumers really
obtained in the best case was skimmed
milk diluted with sugar. No doubt the
effect of competition would be to in-
crease the per-centage of the inferior
constituent. The doctor was more lenient
towards the Australian meat—almost favour-
able to it, in fact. He accounted for the over-
cooking which it undergoes by the excessive
heat required to expel the air from the tins.
To the redeeming quality in its process of
preparation he did full justice. It is neither
roasted nor boiled, but stewed in the best
possible way in its own gravy. Its peculiarity
of flavour was partly a consequence of the
over-cooking, and partly a result of the
reduction of the solid matter into fibrous
particles. Liebig's extract he mildly charac-
terized as a fashionable delusion—meat without
meat. In a sink-room its value was to be
compared with that of stimulants like tea and
coffee, not with nutritive substances like
properly-cooked beef tea.

•
A discussion followed, in reply to which
the learned doctor declared that he had not
intended to do more than state the exact
economic value of the articles ho described.
The other considerations which had been
adduced were also very important, but too
much had been made of the advcantage
Australian meat had over fresh meat in respect
of bone and cooking. That supplied to public
institutions under contract, cost, without bone,
about the same price as Australian meat-7d.
per lb. In private families there was a loss
through the bone, but it should be remem-
bered that the bone itself had a value equal
to a third of the price of meat. The all...ged
saving of fuel did, not practically occur, as
they always required fire for other cooking.

articles.title: TRADES INTELLIGENCE AND LABOUR NEWS. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENTS.]
articles.text:
TRADES INTELLIGENCE
AND LABOUR NEWS.
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENTS.]

IVYCOMBE.

THE CILAIUMAKERS.

For some time the Wycombe chair trade has
shared in the general excitement among all trades;
and the men are seeking an advance of wages.
Their first movement was to organize a union, and
draw up a list of prices, and the masters were
invited to meet the men and discuss the items.
The masters met together; but, instead of resolv-
ing to meet the men in conference on their pro-
posed list, rejected the men's list, and issued one
of their own. Meanwhile the men of one of the
firms were withdrawn by the union, and this was
met by the masters by a lock-out in the cases of
20 or 30 firms. Then came a question of
arbitration; but, meanwhile, this was rendered
almost impossible by the fact that some eight or
ten of the masters had accepted the men's list,
and continued working. The men say they are
willing to modify and define their list; but refuse
arbitration, which might reduce the prices already
accepted by some of the oldest and largest firms
in the town. There are now some 300 or, 400
men "out."

articles.title: LOWESTOFT. STRIKE OF SEAMEN.
articles.text:
LOWESTOFT.
STRIKE OF SEAMEN.

The seamen of Lowastoft engaged in the coal
trade have struck for an advance of 10s. on the
present wages of n 10s. per voyage, the average
length being a month. The boatowners have
resisted the demand, and during the past week
no sailings have been reported from this port. On
Saturday afternoon a number of sailors who had
been engaged in London arrived by train to man
the vessels Betty, Lord Exmouth, and Alma. The
Lowestoft men endeavoured to prevent the crews
from entering upon their duties, and a riot ensued,
which resulted in seine of the London men being
taken into custody. The schooners Lord Exmouth
and Alma succeeded in putting to sea.

SUFFOLK.
lIE SILK WEAVERS.

On Alonday there was a demonstration of the
silk and velvet weavers residing in Sudbury,
Suffolk. About 200 of the men turned out, and
walked in procession through the streets and
neighbourhood. An open air meeting was held
at which letters vere read from operatives in
Halstead, Coggeshall, Ilaverhill, and Shoreditch
(London), stating that the time was come when
there ought to be an advance on the wages paid,
and announcing the intention to agitate for an
increase. They urged the Sudbury operatives to
co-operate with them, so that there might be
united action. Several men were appointed a
deputation to wait on the managers of the fac-
tories with a view-of obtaining higher wages and
the redress of certain grievances in the trade
complained of. The men demand 13 per yard
advance on all narrow plain works, 2d. per yard
on all wide ditto, 3d. on all velvets up to 1,200
" wires," 4d. on ditto of 1,300, 1,400 and 1,500
wires, and 6d. on 1,600 and upwards. They also
contend that they /Ira entitled to compensation for
lois of time and trouble in making up bad
materials.

PRESTON.
TILE STON EMMONS.

The master stonemasons of Preston, in order to
conciliate their men, who struck work a few weeks
ago for an advance of (hi. per day, and extra pay
as mileage when working in the country, have
offered to give the advance in February next, but
the mon have refused to accept this concession,
and offered to give up the demand for extra
country pay, if tho advance per day were granted
at once. This was refused by the masters, and
the strike remains as it was.

DUBLIN.
THE BAKERS' STRIKE.

The want of sufficient bakers' bread was felt
very generally throughont Dublin on Wednesday,
especially by the poorer classes. Flour for
domestic baking was purchased at . an extra-
ordinary rate in the bread shops, where it was
ranged in parcels on the shelves hitherto occupied
by loaves.
A meeting, attended by over 1,500 men,
was held on Wednesday night in the Mechanic's
Institute, under the auspices of the United Trades
Association, at which it was resolved that the
operatives should hold out firmly until their
demand should have been conceded in fu'l.
A Press Association telegmo says the strike has
caused a "complete
,bread famine. Not a single
loaf was to be had, and bread riots are appre-
hended."

BIRKENHEAD.
TILE ENGINEERS' STRIKE.
A meeting of the men belonging to the steam.,
engine makers' association, who came out on
strike at Birkenhead with the other turners,
pattern-makers, &c., about three weeks ago, was
held on Monday. After some discussion, it wai
resolved to accept the offer of the masters of an
advance of 2s. a week all round, and to resume
work on Tuesday morning. The steam-engine
makers' association is not a large body, but it is
said that several non-society men will also go to
work. Last week a number of maohinemen who
had been out on strike resumed employment on
the terms offered by the masters.

LIVERPOOL.
THE BOILER MAKERS.

On Monday, the Loyal Duncombe Lodge of the
No. 2 Branch of Boilermakers and Iron Ship
Builders held their anniversary at Hale, and after
amusing themselves in the village, the party
assembled in a spacious tent erected in a field at
the Wellington Hotel, and partook of an:excellent
dinner. After dinner a short address was given by
the Chairman, Mr. Rushton. After dancing on
the green and other amusements terminated, they
left Hale for Liverpool amidst the cheers of a large
crowd of by-standers.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWF.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWF.

DUBLIN.—Owing to the strike of the operative
bakers a great many of the principal bakery
establishments were closed on Monday, and all
business suspended. As a consequence much in-
convenience was experienced by the public. The
Scotch operatives brought by the masters returned
to Glasgow on Monday.

STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.--410 china and
earthenware manufacturers in the Staffordshire
Potteries have added 10 per cent. to prices, and
the workpeople have given notice of a demand for
a large increase of wages in November.
ROCIIDALE.—On Monday afternoon a meeting
of the fulling millers of Rochdale and district was
held in the Temperance Hall, Rochdale, to con-
sider the reports from their employers as to an
advance of 121 per cent. on their present rate of
wages, and to leave off work at one o'clock on
Saturdays in the place of two. The workpeople
also solicit "That we only work two hours for a
quarter of a day in overtime, four hours for the
half day, and so on. The number now on strike
is between 400 and 500.

TiommitTn.—On Saturday afternoon a demon-
stration in which the weavers at present on strike
in the Holmfirth district, numbering about 900,
took part, together with a large number of
weavers in Huddersfield district who sympathised
with them, was held on the fair ground, Hudders-
field. The weavers from Holmfirth had walked to
Huddersfield along the turnpike road, and at
Lockwood they were joined by the Huddersfield
weavers, and, headed by a brass band, marched in
procession order to Huddersfield. At the fair
ground a large number of people assembled, and
resolutions were passed pledging the men to stand
out until their demands were conceded.

Mr. Gabriel Cox, 93 years of age, residing
in Warberry-lane, Devon, expired a day or
two since from the effects of a blow. About
six weeks ago he was walking in Warberry-
lane when a field gate, which was unhung.to
be repaired, fell against him and knocked him
down. He was assisted home by Mr.
Sampson, dairyman, and others, and died
from the shock to the nervous system.

On Wednesday afternoon about 300 mem-
bers of the British Association celebrafed the
close of the congress at Brighton by a grand
&joiner in the Pavilion. The Mayor occupied
the chair, and the seat of honour at his right
hand was filled by Mr. Stanley, whose health
was received with enthusiasm. The enter-
prising American delivered a charseteristie
speech in reply. The congress of 1872 appears
to have been eminently successful, the number
of tickets issued being 2,533.

The Xttora Roma of Tuesday evening
asserts that the Jesuits, at the last moment,
came to an understanding with the represen-
tatives of the Government charged with the
expropriation of their convent, and that,
consequently, the rumoured protests attributed
to the Jesuits are devoid of foundation, aud
the expropriation was carried out with per-
fect order.

Mr. R. A. Ogilvie, one of the Surveyors General of her Majesty's Customs, is to receive
the honour of a Civil Companionship of the
Rath, in recognition of his long and distin-
gaished servicos. it will be remembered that
Mr. Ogilvie rendered -able assistance during
the negotiations connected with the Interna-
tional Sugar Convention of 18114, as well as
the Commercial Treaty with France.

articles.title: LONDON CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CARPENTERS.

The central committee-room of the carpenters
and joiners at the Brown Bear was thronged all
day on Monday by the men on strike making
anxious inquiries whether any communication
had been received by the committee from Mr.
Bird, the secretary of the masters, appointing a
period when the proposed negotiations would be
reopened and the deputation received. As the day
wore no and on letter came considerable dissatis-
faction was expressed, and the committee were
repeatedly asked what course of action they
intended to adopt, as it was useless wasting any
more time over the subject, the delay and un-
certainty which had already occurred having
injured the movement. To these solicitations the
committee replied that they were prepared to do
their duty and had formed their line of action,
but that they should await the result of the day
before taking any further steps. If any reply
came, and it was not satisfactory, or in any way
evasive, the fact, with the policy intended to be
taken by the committee, would at once be made
known to the men through the medium of the
district committees.

It was afterwards officially communicated to
Mr. C. Matkin, the Carpenters' and Joiners' sec-
retary, that a meeting of the General Committee of
the Central Association of Master Builders wa
ccnvened for Thursday, to consider the re-opening
o f negotiations for a settlement of the dispute;
and it is to be hoped that the employers and the
men may be very shortly once more face to face
endeavouring to make up their differences.
The Central Committee of Carpenters and
Joiners have struck and paid a dividend for the
past week at the rate of 16s. per man for Jackson
and Shaw's and Brass's bands, and 13s. for tho
remainder, being an advance of Is. 6d. in each
case upon the previous week; but Mr. Matk in
the secretary, acting under instructions from his
committee, refused to furnish any estimate of the
number of recipients, beyond this that they were
now confined to the " aristocracy " of. the trade.
He was, moreover, directed to intimate that such
inquiries betrayed impertinent public curiosity, as
the glispute was now narrowed to a more domestic
limit.

A special meeting of the central committee of
carpenters and joiners was held on Tuesday at the
Brown Bear, Broad-street, Bloomsbury, and was
attended by delegates from some of the districts.
Mr. Makin, the secretary, read a letter from the
assistant secretary of the Master Builders' Asso-
ciation, stating that a specially summoned meeting
of the general committee of the association would
be held on Thursday next, when the letters from
the central committee, enclosing a copy of the
resolution of the carpenters' delegates would be
taken into consideration, and a time fixed for
receiving the carpenters' deputation, armed with
full powers to treat for a settlement of the dispute.
The committee then proceeded to arrange the
deputation, and it was decided, subject to any
alteration required by the terms of the letter from
the committee of masters, that the deputation
should consist of at least five members, the
responsibility being considered too great to be
intrusted to a less number. The instructions
under which the deputation were to act were then
discussed, but the decision on the question was
not made known.

Upon the questions of time and wages there
will not be much danger of the negotiations
falling through, although no doubt both points
will be sharply contested on either side. The real
danger will be in reference to the code of working
rules, regulating overtime and its payment, and
dealing with the vexed question of piecework.
The carpenters and joiners, unlike the masons,
attach more importance to a code of working rules
than to the points of hours and wages, arguing that
a good code of rules would regulate both those
questions. On the other hand, the masters, or at
least a large and influential section among them,
entertain a strong objection to being bound to hard
and fast lino such as a code of ..ules would pro-
duce. Hence the danger of a hitch in the
negotiations upon this point, and which will only
be prevented by concessions on both sides. There
is this to be said in favour of a code of working
rules—that they exist, more or less, in the build-
ing trade in nearly every provincial town, and,
with few exceptions, have been found to work
satisfactorily to both employers and workmen.
Messrs. Burgess and Benny, the two members
of the committee, who have been away for the
last month on a deputation in Lancashire, returned
home on Wednesday morning, and gave in their
report to the committee. They had attended 12
public meetings in as many of the principal towns
in the country, visited all the local and other
societies, and different trades' councils, and have
established committees in every town ,they have

visited. They had everywhere been well received,
and, as a rule, in each place they had visited a
weekly levy of 6d. had been agreed.
The central committee has issued its printed
audited balance-sheet for the month of July, from
which it appears that, including the balance from
previous months of £166, the total income of the
strike fund for two months had amounted to
£2,914 16s. 6id., and the expenditure to £2,602
Os. 6id., leaving in hand a balance at the end of
the month of £312 Bs. The receipts are made up of
the 38. weekly levy from London men in work, of
voluntary contributions from the carpenters and
other trade societies, and of the subscriptions from
committees formed in several of the provincial
towns, but the great bulk of the amount is from
the carpenters alone. The expenditure consists of
£2,361 17s. 2d., being pay for four weeks to the
men on strike, and £240 11s. 4id., for payment
and expenses of committees, delegations, printing,
stationery, and other miscellaneous items, being
at the rate of £6O per week.
On Wednesday evening the Grecian or City-
road Theatre was crowded, the performances
being for the benefit of the men on strike, a cir-
cumstance which caused a general desertion of
the Brown Boar and the other resorts of the trade.
The dispute has come to be described as exceed-
ingly complicated. By accident, the title of the
principal drama was singularly appropriate to such
a state of affairs, viz., "The Tangled Skein ;
Mystery." A prologue, "written expressly for
the occasion," was recited, in which the position
and claims of the benefoiers was thus referred to:
To strike or not ! The strike, that is the question.
We're open to any fair suggestion.

T* *- .-- • *
Born to work, and wed to tred disasters,
We're levelled down in levelling up our masters.
What boots our skill, if we are without ambition
To make our trade a ladder to position ?

"Union is strength." When workmen pull to-
gether,
They need not fear old age or rainy weather.
"Chip of a block" whose roots are deep and
olden,
Our grand old charter is unstained and golden.
Our guild dates back to early mystic ages,
And on its scroll we've martyrs and we've sages.

articles.title: LONDON PAINTERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON PAINTERS.

A delegate meeting of painters was held on
Friday evening at the Three Doves, Berwick-
street; Mr. Shipton in the chair. The business
consisted of reviewing the proceedings of the past
week at Messrs. Waller's firm and also as to the
attainment of the terms of their memorial. It was
agreed to pay fifteen shillings as a dividend to the
men on strike. All the hands withdrawn from
Messrs. Waller's have found work elsewhere. The
following resolution was put and carried.
That in consequence of the complete success of
the strike at Messrs. Waller and Son's of Pimlico,
the committee are requested to open communica-
tions with the men in one or two other firms with
a view to call out the men.

After some other routine business the meeting
adjourned.
A public meeting of operative house painters and
decorators, at which all their societies wore repre-
sented, was held on Monday at the Three Doves
Tavern, Berwick-atrect, Soho, to consider the
expediency of re-opening negotiations with the
employers. Mr. Cicero Shipton occupied the
chair, and after giving an explanation of
the altered :aspect Of affairs, he left it for the
trade to determine.,;what should be done.
Mr. Gahagan moved,
.and Mr. Watkins
seconded :7--•

That the meeting do re-affirm the resolution
passed some Limo since, viz., that we appoint two
delegates to negotiate with the Masters' Associa-
tion, with full power to conclude terms of the
conditions under which we are to work in future ;
and to act either independently or in conjunction
with other branches of the building trade.

An amendment was ploposed that before this
step was taken :an aggregate meeting should be
bold at Cumbridge-hall, Newman-street, Oxford-
street, which obtained only seven votes, and the
original resolution having been declared carried by
an overwhelming majority, Messrs. Shipton and
Phillips wore r,3-olected the ;delegates to put it in
force.

The painters' committee intend calling out their
men from Messrs. Holland and Hannon's, the tirm
refusing to pay on the terms of the memorial.

articles.title: LONDON BRICKLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BRICKLAYERS.

A crowded meeting of the Operative Brick-
layers' Society took place on Monday night at the
Sussex Hotel, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, in
relation to the existing dispute in the building
trade.

Tho Chairman said they were all aware of the
position of the present dispute, and how their
trade was affected by it. They had at present
three firma under strike, and the council had

called this meeting to take the opinion of the
members as to whether it would be desirable to
strike three more of the largest and busiest firms
in the trade, in support of the full terms of their
memorial, or appoint a deputation to meet the
masters, with full power to treat for a settlement.
Mr. Coulson, the secretary, having detailed the
operations of the strike committee up to this date,
said the men on strike had been well and efficiently
supported. _

A long and animated discussion ensued, during
which the general feeling of the meeting was
unequivocally expressed against the policy of
sending any further deputation to the masters.
The following resolutions were ultimately almost
unanimously adopted:

Ist. That we maintain our stand for the nine
hours and ninepence, with a code of working
rules.

2nd. That we take immediate action with three
other firms until we obtain a settlement of the
present dispute.

The carrying into effact the second [resolution
was left to the council, but the firms selected are
to be struck at once.

At a meeting of the bricklayers' committee, held
on Tuesday morning, at the Bell, Old Bailey, it
was resolved to strike the firm of Henshaw and
Co., and accordingly at the dinner hour on that
day the whole of the bricklayers working on the
various jobs of the firm, including two large build-
ings in the city, were called out, and obeyed the
call to a man. Two other of the large firms will
be struck to-day.

articles.title: LONDON AMALGAMATED BUILDING TRADES COMMITTEE.
articles.text:
LONDON AMALGAMATED
BUILDING TRADES COMMITTEE.

On Tuesday night the Amalgamated Building
Tradeb' Committee re-assembled at the White
Rose, Castle-street, Leicester-square, when the
prospect of an early compromise was as eagerly
canvassed as it had been in the camp of the
seceding carpenters and joiners. Every delegate,
with the exception of the bricklayers, came fur-
nished with a written authority to assent to any
joint action that might be agreed upon for re-
opening negotiations with the Central Associa-
tion of Master Builders; and on the motion of
Mr. 'Halloran (labourer), seconded by Mr. Vivian
(metal worker), the following resolution was
agreed to, Tiz. :
That our secretary be empowered to communi-
cate with Mr. Stanley Bird, requesting hint to be
good enough to arrange some convenient time on
an early date tor a meeting of the Committee of
the Master Builders' Association and a deputation
from this committee representing the plasterers,
painters, metal-workers, and labourers, with a
view to the settlement of the present dispute, such
deputation having full power from their consti-
tuents to effect the same.

articles.title: JOURNEYMEN BAKERS OF LONDON.
articles.text:
THE JOURNEYMEN BAKERS OF
LONDON.

Several large and important meetings of the
London operative and journeymen bakers have
been held in various parts of the metropolis.
The men appear to have a wholesome prejudice
against striking, and in many instances greatly
blame the Eastend operatives for their premature
movement. The groat majority of the East-end
bakers, however, are Germans, and are under the
guidance of a German society.
At a meeting held on Saturday at the Temper-
ance Hall, Trafalgar-street, Walworth, Mr. E.
Adams, secretary of the council, in the chair, a
delegate was appointed to attend the meeting
next week to perfect the arrangements for meet-
ing the masters in conference. The chairman
referred to the present position of the trade, and
said the trade had never been in a more favourable
position. On every hand they had heard of
strikes; but he thought the course the bakers were
taking in arranging to meet their employers was
far better than any strike (hear, hoar.) He
thought the terms the men demanded were fair
and reasonable, and were for the benefit of the
employers as well as the men. Ho persuaded his
employer to do away with night work some years
ago, and now he would not return to it under
any circumstances (cheers.) At the present time
if all the young men in London were to turn out
there were enough boys who had a slight know-
ledge of the trade to fill their places. With regard
to the conference it was the most practical thing
to do, as the employers wished it as well as the
men, for they saw there must be a reform in that
trade.
Mr. G. Strickland then moved—.

That this meeting of journeymen and operative
bakers views with feeliw.rs of the greatest satis-
faction the approaching conference between
masters and men, and sincerely trusts it will not
be unattended with good results.

The resolution was seconded by Mr. Chaplain
and carried.

Another meeting was held at the Greyhound

Hotel, under the auspices of No. 8 Branch, Mr.
Joseph Gill in the chair. The secretary, Mr. G.
Gunning, reported attending the meeting of the
trades council, and read the platform of principles.
He also reported that 100 master bakers had
already spontaneously done away with Sunday
labour, a statement which was received with
demonstations of delight. Mr. Gunning also stated
that a largo number of undersellers' shops in the
south of London had made an advance in price,
which was considered a step in the right direction.
A series of resolutions which wore adopted at the
last meeting of the Bermondsey and Rotherhithe
Master Bakers' Association, was also read to the
meeting. They were to the effect that the whole
of the masters should be in one union, and the
whole of the men in another; the employers to
determine not to employ a non-society man, and
the journeymen to refuse to work for an employer
who was not a member of the Trade Protection
Society. These resolutions were approved of, and
a resolution was also adopted as follows :
That this meeting of journeymen and operative
bakers approve of the business transacted at tho
trades council, and, having full confidence in
their delegate, pledge themselves to abide by the
decision of the council.

A larBe meeting was also held at the Woolman
Tavern, Forest-row, Kingsland, more especially to
consider the total abolition of night work in the
baking trade. The chair was occupied by Mr.
Hooker, who, in opening the proceedings expressed
his pleasure at seeing such a large attendance,
comprising three-fourths of the journeymen of
Singsland, Balaton, llornsoy, and Stoke Newing-
ton, With regard to the wages question ho was
satisfied nothing would be done unless a stated
price for labour was laid down, and proposed the
following:—
That no foreman, second hand, or third hand
work under 30s. 245., and 20s. respectively ; and
that no Scotch iorehand or single band work for
less than 265. per week, and that Sunday bakiags
be abolished.

Mr. Evershed seconded, and dwelt at some
length upon tbo question at issuo. He contentlQ.l
that as the price of labour had been for a consider-
able time on the rise, through the increased wealth
and trade of the country, they as journeymen had
a right to demand their share of the prospoi ity
with which the country abounded. The propoii-
tion was carried, and Mr. Howe, president of the
eouncil, addressed the meeting, and exhorted the
men to stand by the union and all would go on
well. Mr. Cossey, Mr. Dunn, Mr. Grattan (from
Ireland), and others addressed the meeting, ant
a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the pro-
ceedings to a close.

The committee of the Master Bakers' Trade
Protection Society mot in great strength on Wo,!_
nesday at its offices in Fetter-lane, Mr. Dwarber
in the chair, to consider the question of conference
with the journeymen. The men's platform of
principles was discussed, and after various opinions
had been expressed, the following resolutions
were passed, to be brought before the meeting of
members :

1. That a working day shall consist of 12 hours,
and not commence before 4 o'clock a.m.
2. That the committeo sea no means of
abolishing Sunday bakings except by Act. of
Parliament. 4V
3. That tho third proposition of the men, that a
universal rise of 3s. per man should be given,
cannot be entertained.

4. That yeast money, bread, flour, and all other
perquisites be abolished, and the wages of the
operative be paid according to his worth.
ö. That overtime shall be charged at per
hour.

Mr. Rose then moved, and Mr. Ayton, seconded
the resolution—

That Mr. Treman Hare be invited to take the
chair at the conference, subject to On approval cl
the men.

The above conditions will be discussed
shortly at a meeting of masters and men, and it
appears, from trustworthy information, that the
masters will hold out against the indiscriminato
pay of three shillings, and a great many in regard
to the abolition of Sunday bakings—a source of
profit little bakers rely upon, and which would
deprive thousands of the London working classes
of a hot dinner on Sunday. The sack money, too,
is a payment the bakers' wives will strenuously
object to forfeit. The men at present are split
up into three societies. 1. The Amalgarna'ed
Union of Operative Baker:, the central office being
at Manchester. 2. The London Union General
Board. 3. The Germans at the East-end. Tho
masters are more combined in a General Trade

MEETING AT YEOVIL.

A meeting was held in the Yeovil Cattle,Market
on Saturday evening, in connection with the
National Agricultural Labourers' Union. Mr.
George Potter, the well-known unionist, presided,
and there was a very large gathering of artisans,
tradesmen, and labourers. -
In the course of his opening remarks the Chair-
man said that the union had boon formed for the
purpose of enabling labourers in husbandry to
obtain an advance of wages, a reduction of working
hours, and better houses to live in. He then
spoke of the vast improvements which had taken
place in the condition of the artisan class and the
farmers during the past twenty years, and urged
those of his hearers who followed agricultural
pursuits to unite together for the purpose of im-
proving their condition. Having quoted statistics
to prove that the wealth of the country was
increasing rapidly year by year, he reminded the
labourers that they were the producers of that
wealth, and that they were the only class of the
cOmmunity who had not shared in the general
Prosperity. - According to one Of the agricultural
journds, he said, the wages paid in Somerset
were less than in any other county in Eng!and,
averaging from Bs. to 10s. per week Only, while in
many other counties as much as 165.; lOs., and

lt3s. per week had been paid fir a long time past
After dilating at considerable length upon the
miserable condition of the working men in the
rural districts, Mr. Potter referred to the remarks
recently made by the Bishop of Gloucester and
Bristol, respecting the agricultural labourer&
movement, nild in an elognent speech answered
the Bishop's truthless statements.

Mr. George Mitchell, "One from the Plough,"
then gave his experiences as a labourer, and
described the faro of which he then partook. He
repeated his intention to carry on the agi-
tation 'until the labourers were better paid.
People in Peterborough and London would- not
believe what he had stated as to the wages
and homes of the Somerset labourers. Captain
Swann, at Lyme Regis, said that he and
others were anxious
.to do away with the army
and navy. There was no truth in the state-
ment. Ile was as loyal as anyone, and was proud
of his country, but he was not proud of the half-
starved labourers. Ile trusted that God would
grant him two requests, that he should live to see
the elevation of the farm labourers' of Somerset,
and that he should have the con-tant power of
doing good. (Cheers.)
Mr. Barnett proposed the following resolu-
tion :

That this meeting is of opinion that a branch of
the National Agricultural Labourers' Union should
be formed at Yeovil for the purpose of improving
the condition of the labourers present, and believes
it to be the duty of all labourers present to join it
and to urge their fellow labourers to unite with
them to obtain a rise of wages.
The speaker detailei the progress of the move-
ment in•Dorsetshire, and sad that it 4 success had
been marvellous. At Winfrith 109 members joined
at one meeting. One man, 40 years of age, said
he only received 63. a weak, an] is. out of that
was deducted for rent.

Mr. James Burt, a labourer, seconded the reso-
lution, and stated that ho only received 73. a
week.

'• Mr. Toseph Arch, after speaking of the subject
generally, remarked that if the Bishop of Glou-
cester and Bristol supposed that the labourers
were placed on some Alpian height, from whence

to which they. could descend at leisure, he was
vastly mistaken, and. he most sincerely wished
that it were Poisible for his lordship to exchange
places with one of 'them for twelve months.
(Hear, hear.) The Bishop and those who thought •
with him disliked unionizing, alleging that it
fostered strife, and that thera was a lot of rattening
amongst those who joined together for the purpose
of obtaining hotter Pay. The only strife was
that caused by the refusal on the part of the
employers to meet the just demands or the men;
but with respect to rattening it was a very common
thing in 'every day life. :Why, even clergymen
did is little of it at times.
,(Lfaughter.) lie (NU%
Arch) was at Ross a short time ago, and while •
there he was requested to prettah in the Town
Hall. He consented; but lo and behold, he
received a lawyer's letter, saying that if his dared
to do so he must expect to abide by the con-
sequences. He did
.preach, nevertheless, and
that, too, to about 2,000 persons. (Applause.)
Lawyers would not allow Men to practice in the

of the district joined the union there could be no

Mr. Benjamin Taylor, high bailiff of Peter.
borongh, then addressed the meeting at consider-
able length, a vein of banter running through the
whole of his speech. Ho remarked that he was a
very loyal man, and he could not see the necessity
for saying so many hard thingsabout those who held

the love of
.money was the root of all evil, and if
that was true, the labourers owed a deep debt
.of
gratitude to the Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol
and all the other bishops, for they removed a good
deal out of their way. (Laughter.) if it was
correct, as he had read in the good old Book, that
it was easier for a camel to get through the eye of
a needlo than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom
of Heaven, the poverty-stricken sons of toil might
well be thankful that riches would not keep them

.employers even if they could do

.to stay in the parishes

he have thought, he might ask, had anyone
preached that doctrine to him when he was aiming

at his present position. But then, of course, bishops

go ! " (Roars of laughter.)

Cheers were then given for Mr. George Mitchell

Thirty-two branches are reported by the district

and scores are joining every week. The greatiest
Prekidices have to be battled with; both viith
masters and men. To say nothing of the commen
usage of day labour, instead of by task work,

ment, which makes the value of p.iyinent, to range

A meeting was held on Tuesday night in the
Chequers publichouse, High-street, Oxford, and

the sending by Government of a Iliers into look-
out districts in Oxfordshire. The chair was taken

because of the difference with his master. The
meeting was also addressed by Mr. Tennant, Mr.

following resolution was unanimously adopted
That we, the working-men of Oxford, feel the
injustice done to the agricultural labourerin this
county by the employment of the military at
harvest work. We feel ourselves bound to mit
our senior member, the Right Hon. Edward
Cardwell, 43 Secretary of War, for the immediate
withdrau al and recall of the soldiers. '

There were about 300 persons present; and the
proceedings" were unanimous.

THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH

SERVICE.

POST OFFICE AND TUE SORTERS' GRIEVANCES.

Finding that, owing to the high price of pro-
visions, house reut, and all articles of general
consumption, their wages were insufficient in
February last, petitions were sent to the Post-
master-General from the various branches by the
sorters, sub-sorters, etc. (or as they are now de-
signated "indoor officers") in London. They
having waited patiently for some months, and not
having, in most cases, had any acknowledgment
for the receipt of their petitions, caused enquiries
to be made of the Controller of the circulation
office, who stated, through the Sub-Controller,
• that a, new scale Would shortly be issued, and
possibly it would be satisfactory, so as to render
an interview with the Controller unnecessary.
This new scale, or to give it its proper name,
"revised scale," was 13.rst published at the district
offices, and caused general dissatisfaction, which
coming to their knowledge, and receiving invita-
tions to join with the letter carriers in sending
delegates to wait.on the Postmaster. General, they
accordingly acquiesced.

The Postmaster-General, after receiving a letter
from the secretary to the delegates (who is a sub-
sorter), returned word that he could only see the
lettemarriers.

Fife' Of' the delegates then waited upon the
Controller, and solioited him to advise the Post.
master-General to receive the whole of the dele-
gates, viz., the sorters, sub-sorters, assistants, and
porters with the- letter-carriers. The Controller
informed the deputation that he could not do so.
It was then resolved (the men wishing to pursue
a conciliatory policy) that the letter-carriers should
see the Postmaster-General by themselves, the
result of which interview has been already noticed
In these columns. , •

The Secretary of-the delegates has since been
informed that if the "indoor officers" desired an
interview with the Postmasti3r-General, that appli-
cations must be made from each branch separately.
This answer gives great dissatisfaction, as the
men can see that the authorities are trying to
. .
destroy theiunison of feeling, so that they may be
able to defeat the men in detail.
The indoor officers' time of attendance is 4.45
a.m., to 8.30 or 9 a.m., if required, and from 4.45
p.m. to 8 p.m. These are not long hours if the
men had only one attendance per diem, but having
to walk twiee home and back, and many of the
men being compelled by the high rentals to live
three or more miles from the office, this extra
• attendance should, be considered as two hours
work, and the fact of the men while in the office
having to ViOrk, IlndeY the high-pressure and
sgaipst time, is ituite: ignored by the authorities,
also is:the fact of the men only
.heing able to
olitain one fair night's rest, per week. Owing to
the bulk of the correspondence arriving at the
(nee at stated times, it requires active men to
deal with it, to prevent the delay of the mails,
There are many young sorters who have been in
the servied from eight to twelve years who do not
receive more than 30s. por week, and, having
young families, they are glad. to obtain' work
between the hours that the office does not require
their servicèa o that they may he able to pay
their, way, and. provide the common necessaries of
lifelnr:themselves and families. Nally of them
risit. at 3.30 a.m., and with the exception of

all the day, reaching their homes at 9 p.m.,
making 17i hours work a day to obtain a living.
The sorters are told that they are
.entitled to pen-
sions, but the authorities, by keeping them at such
160 wages, and compelling them to work such long
hours to get a bare livelihood, lesson the chances
of their getting pensions. The authorities have
tieve i informed the public Of the very small per-
certtage who: obtain them, because, .if they did, it
Would expose the fallacy. The sorters have al
petitioned for au increase of 10. pee pent. to their
•wages, tnd this revised scale does not give them
one halfpenny. The men consider that this
revised scale is an insult to them, and a very
.bitter feeling is rising, whiela the authorities
should endeavour to allay.
The'sorters aro also told that in 12 years' time
they will receive 458. per week, but that thought
does not relieve their
,present necessities, for as
the old adage has it "While the grass is growing
the steed is starving."

They have complied with the instructions of the
Controller, and have sent applications for an inter-
view with the Postmaster-General, and up to the
time of writing the sorters in the r,tegisfered Letter
Branch are the only ones who have received an
inewer. Their Sub-Controller told them that
the ,Postmaster-Generat had decided not to
reedy° any mere deputations, and as be *wins
about going to {lreland, he the Sub-Controller,

would not forward their application, and accord.:
ingly made them take it back.
Is it necessary that because men are in the
Post-office that they should be dampened to submit
to. this treatment, and that by entering this
service they should forfeit the rights and privileges
of Englishmen?
The administration of the minor establishment
is a national disgrace, for men should be paid a
proper and reasonable price for their work, and
not obligated to work seventeen hours per day, and
the authorities in their new scales, should act
more justly towards them, and not keep all the
benefits on the side of the Post-office.

Ought it to be necessary that while men faith-
fully discharge their duties, that they should be
compelled to resort to violent measures before
their grievances are redressed?
