articles.title: SATURDAY, AUGUST 24, 1872
articles.text:
SATURDAY, AUGUST 24, 1872

ME BUILDERS' STRIKE.

The carpenters and joiners have signified
their readiness to enter into negooiations With
the masters, and are only waiting for their
answer. It is delayed by the absence of the
principal persons from town, at the Lakes, 0r
the sea-side, and in other places of summer
resort. in the Meantime, a portion of thq,
'men drawn out obtain work under other firAti
at reduced -time and increased pay.
complete success Of the strike in certain cool
encourages further attempts. What is going
on outside this and all other trades, makes it
pretty evident, that concession will he inevit-
able. If the employers be reasonable, they
will not find the men impracticable.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
THE military authorities have made them-
selves parties in the dispute between employers
and employed by allowing soldiers to go into
the harvest field, where, though unskilled
hands, they are paid at higher prices than
those which the farmers have refused to their
own villagers. The regulations for the army
provide for the soldiers assisting in the collo-
tion of the harvest, when application is made,
but "provided that the population is not
thereby interfered with." It remains to be
seen what answer the commanding officers wbc
have allowed their men to go into the corn-
fields have to make to the complaint that
they have grievously interfered with the
population. Lord EMMY may dissuade
labourers from losing their independence by
joining the union; but what independence
have they the least chance of unless they do?

THE BALLOT AT PONTEFRACT.
OUR philosophical politicians who look
upon the people as a doubtful material, useful
for the purpose of trying political experiments,
express themselves disappointed with the first
trial of the ballot at Pontefract.
Their reasons are not many, nor can it be
said that they are very satisfactory. Su°ll
persons forecast events in a very strong belief
that they are adepts in politioal scienoe, and
when their predictions are falsified, as the"'
usually are by results, they blame everybodY

concerned but themselves. The Spectator
takes rather a desponding view—because so
few electors voted ;—because Mr. CHILDERS'
re-election would have been certain with open
voting, whilst under the ballot it appears to
have been the result of accident ;—because such
an example as that set by Pontefract in this
instance will deprive us of strong men in
Parliament; because there was no' sound
healthy opinion operating, or there could not
be so close a contest; and because, under open
voting, to have pitted such a man as Lord
POLLINGTON against Mr. CHILDERS would
have been impossible.
It is very well to say all this as comment on
the Pontefract election k When people want to
furnish many reasons against a thing they
know little or nothing about, they are not
usually particular as to their validity or fit-
ness. The history of our elections, however,
shows how utterly from the purpose such talk
is. Lord POLLINGTON as against Mr. CrtrLDEtts
was not a very exciting theme. The disparity
of force is no doubt considerable, and we
admit, without the least hesitation, that it
would have been most discreditable if a young
aristocratic noodle had displaced a capable
man of good experience. But to say that
such a contest could not have taken place
with open voting, is not quite in accordance
with even moderately recent experience. If
we remember rightly, JOIIN BRIGHT was
driven out of Manchester by an open vote;
RICHARD COBDEN Out of Huddersfield; Mr.
EIVART GLADSTONE out of Oxford; Mr.
EDWARD WILLIAM FORSTER out of Leeds;
and JOHN STUART MILL out of Westminster,
by men whose united ability as statesmen
might he fitly limited to the framing of a decent
turnpike Bill, we shall understand ',how un-
tenable such a position is. If the Spectator
will look fairly at such facts, we think it need
not take this Pontefract affair so much to
heart, nor become melancholy, lest our good
strong men should withdraw from Parlia-
mentary life, and taka to retired corners and
sulk because the silly sons of Lords, or it may
be more vulgar persons, sot themselves up
against them as Parliamentary candidates.
Dut our contemporary, whose liberality
Is very honest, though rather
.too daintily
addicted to the" pouncet box, "assures us that
Ned the voting been open, "Lord POLLINOTON
wpuld have retired under the pressure of uni-
versal awl. healthy political opinion. We do
not deny tlae, bnt we believe most strongly
that no more ridiculously foolish statement
ever appeared in the columns of
.a newspaper.
Can the Spectator point to anyone instance in
the history of our Parliamentery elections in
'which the candidature of an idiotic pretender
was rendered impossible by the universal pro-
test of a constituency, in favour of a man of
even the most conspicuous ability or the most
signal public service? We would undertake
on the shortest notice to find scores of instances
of an opposite kind, were it at all possible that
our opinion on this matter was called in ques-
tion, Under open voting in such a borough as
Pontefract a fool with a purse, with active
agents, and.with a disposition not to be stingy,
might drive out of the field the best man in
every way the country could furnish.
Besides, there is an explanation different
from that given by the Spectator for the
abstinence of voters. It is true that that con-

stituenoy consists of 1,900 voters, and that
6 only 1,230 registered their votes. It may be
that some of the 730 abstainers, in keeping
from the poll, acted in a sense of offended
dignity, because they were precluded by
the secret system from exercising their right
as citizens in open day, out before the world
as honest men. Such monsters of honesty
and independence may exist at Pontefract,
but we question very much whether the
Spectator could find 730 such dignified and
delicate-minded persons. If, however,there was
any way of testing the fads, we think we could
find for our contemporary a goodly number of a
very different sort of citizen. We have no doubt
that some of our parliamentary agents—
experienced " men in the moon "—could tell
how many bribable voters there are in Ponta-
fraet. Were they preparing for a campaign
under the open system, they would very
readily "tottle" these up, and tell us how many
Irtight be " tipped " out of this 730; how

many might be made sweet with a young
idiotic lord's "sugar ;" in fact, how many
would be content to take their candidate from
Earlswood if he brought with him a well-
filled purse.
The disgusted men at Pontefract were not,
we fear, the independent men who wanted to
vote openly, but the shabby knaves who had
votes to sell, and who felt no disposition to
put themselves out of the way to go to the
poll for nothing. Instead, therefore, of con.
sidering it a misfortune, or any discredit to the
Ballot, that such persons did not vote, it may be
taken as in favour of secret voting that it
secured their neutrality. We do not say that
the 730 abstainers in Pontefract were all
corrupt men, but we think, without meaning
any offence to the little town, that clever
agents under the old system could have
found 730 amongst the general body of
electors capat le of understanding the value of
a "tip," and willing to accept it, if not dis•
gustingly
We do not believe in heroic voters disposed to
retire offended from secret Parliamentary
contests. We do, however, believe in persons
indifferent to Parliamentary struggles as dis-
gracefully numerous in all constituencies. At
the same time, we are convinced that the
majority of those who, under the Ballot, will
keep aloof from the poll are corrupt persons;
who will not vote because they can neither
get money nor drink for doing so. In this
matter our electioneering practices have
brought us very low. It would be well to
disfranchise such persons; could a safe way
of doing so be discovered? If, however, under
the Ballot they cut themselves off, it is a
matter to be thankful for, not to regret. The
earnest men and the honest men will vote, and
these are the men upon whom the nation can
most safely rely in the ahoice of representa-
tives; and we think that the fact brought
out by the return of Mr. CIIILDERS is credit-
able rather than otherwise to Pontefract, as it
has made clear the fact that there was a clear
majority of 80 in favour of the best man.
If all our other constituencies, when brought
to the test, give us a like result, we shall have
no occasion to find fault with the Ballot. If
from Land's End to John o'Groats we can
find 658 men who vote as they ought to do,
against 578 who run after and shout for
noodles, we shall have much to thank the
Ballot for, and great reason to be hopeful in
regard to the future of the nation.

articles.title: PROTESTANT AND CATHOLIC IN IRELAND.
articles.text:
PROTESTANT AND CATHOLIC IN
IRELAND.

THE relations between Protestant and
Papist in the same countries are rarely much
better than a smouldering fire. Ireland,
north as well as south, never fails to keep up
in the mind the sense of being on the verge
of a volcano, or of walking above the trem-
blings of an earthquake. There are symptoms
stronger than a MURPHY riot, which may,
unless some good genius forefond, make even
England the scene of similar uncomfortable-
ness. It is a great pity that people who per-
suade themselves that they have truth on their
side, and are convinced that truth has that
within it which must cause it to prevail,
cannot rely upon the moral forces, but must
betake themselves to forms of demonstration,
even in the celebration of a holiday, which
have anything but reason and logic in them.
The Orangemen of Derry this time, and not
the first, began the proceedings which have
thrown into confusion that city of Ireland
whose normal condition ought to be one, for
its own credit's sake, of exemplary quiet and,
self-control. Had not the Boys of the Maiden
City indulged themselves with keeping their
party anniversary by making ostentatious
displays, perhaps the Catholics who are mixed
among the Ulster population would net have
been stimulated to manifestations of an
opposite nature on the nearest following holy
day of their religion.
Nevertheless, a heavy responsibility hangs
upon those, whoever they may be, that were
at the bottom of that opposite outburst.
Before the day on which the Church of Rome
observes "the Feast of the Assumption of
Our Lady," public notice was paraded by a
committee, that, the Party Processions Act
having been repealed, the Catholics of Derry

would hold "a monster demonstration," first
hearing mass and afterwards going in proces-
sion through the streets. Hearing of this,
their brethren in Downshire resolved to follow
the example, assembling at Gilfrid. The
Protestants of the country, therefore, made up
their minds to meet them. Catching the
inflammatory infection, the partisans of
Nationalism and Home Rule, determined not
to be behindhand, but to assemble in force.
Hannah's-town was the rendezvous first an-
flounced; but, unhappily, the final rallying.
point was changed to Belfast.

This last movement was the only one that
avowed an object, namely, to call upon
Government to set free the Fenian convicts.
When the Orangemen declared their inten-
tion to give the Rome Rulers the meeting,
peaceable persons took the alarm. Applica-
tions were made for protection, and military as
well as police had orders to concentrate them-
selves upon the point threatened with disorder.
The event has more than justified the
apprehensions. In 1865, Belfast was the
theatre of similar scenes, in which lives
were lost, men and women wounded by
the hundred, and property laid waste,
ending in the occupation of the town by
thousands of soldiers with artillery. On the
present occasion, the processioning on one day
led to rioting the next. On Friday there was
a regular battle betwixt the counter demon-
strators. The bruised and wounded were
many, some with serious effects, from the
sword-cuts of the police. Bad went on to
worse. By Monday last the town was mani-
festly beyond the power of the local magistracy
to deal with. The inhabitants were warned to
keep indoors; the publiohouses were shut, and
the police and soldiery had orders which all
but placed the town in a state of siege.
Plunder and destruction set in, Catholic shop-
keepers being apparently the chief sufferers.
The Catholic rioters, in return, beat every
person in the street who refused to cross him-
self ; and, in short, all the force collected
could not prevent a succession of fights the
whole day long. There was less disturbance
on Tuesday; not, however, because much real
progress had been made in the positive re-
pression of the factions. On the contrary,
wrecking was resumed by those calling them-
selves Protestants, who, as fast as they were
checked by the military in one district, made
off to another. The arrivals of constabulary
and military was so numerous as to suggest a
fear lest other places should be stripped of
guards against outbreak. The local magis-
trates began to fear the consequences to
themselves of being seen at points where the
men carrying arms might be ordered to fire
upon the rioters. The fall of a constable by a
shot gave occasion to an order that the police
and the soldiers should charge the whole
mob at the point of the bayonet. On Wednes-
day morning matters were less disquiet, and
the multiplication of arrests, in set-off against
wounds and injuries on all sides, seemed to
show that the authorities were at last getting
the upper hand.

It would be doing the working men of
Belfast a great injustice not to state, on the
respectable authority of the Northern Whig,
that the Protestant mob consisted mainly of
the mere roughs of the town and port, and
that the intelligent and sober artisans, who
are numerous and influential, stood aloof. The
recurrence of such scenes in a town like
Belfast is certainly disgraceful. Considering
its intelligenoe, activity, and wealth, it ought
to be the last place in Ireland to be given up
to:confusion and disorder. For the same
reasons that make Glasgow and Liverpool
peaceful and orderly, the (thief town of Ulster
ought to be a model of respect for law and
security. And yet, for similar if not identical
reasons, not only those great ports of England
and Scotland, but many of our large towns,
are, on occasion, as liable as Belfast itself to
outbreaks of factious hostility, exasperated by
denominational war-cries. Perhaps, indeed,
the Protestants of Belfast are more apt to
over-estimate their numerical strength. We
remember being strongly assured by one of
these, that there was not a South Irishman in
all the town. Of course, this was not likely
to be literally true; but the mere making of
such an assertion raises a certain presumption

as to the prevailing sentiment. What, however,
the Catholic element is to Belfast, that the
Irish element is to English end Scotch towns
of any size ani importance. We need not
call it an ever-present danger, but it certainly
is one among other conditions and circum-
stances never to be left out of account in any
calculation made with a view to the preserva-
tion of neighbourly feeling and the main-
tenance of social harmony.
If mere legislation could keep the peace,
Parliament has done enough to secure order in
either Belfast or Cork. But, unfortunately,
acquiescence in this view does not rest with
either the Protestants in the one or the
Catholics in the other. Generally sneaking,
the last men to be seen in mobs are those who
set them on. It is perfectly true that the
mixing up of religion and politics has much to
answer for on occasions like the present. The
disestablishment and disendowment of the
Irish Church ought, no doubt, to have contented
the Catholic majority; but, while there was not
the same obvious reason for its making the
Orangemen happy, there were influential
persons, on the other side, in whom, far front
causing an eternal repletion, it did but whet the
appetite for more. At this moment, the PRIXEE
MINISTER of England might do what no other
power can just now accomplish for a general
pacification, so far as that lies within human
reach. It is doubtful, however, whether even
the term of Christmas will find Mr. OLA.DSTONE
prepared to put an end to that suspense of
which, it is plain, Cardinal CULLEN and others
are bent on taking every advantage. The
expulsion of Jesuits from Germany appears
to be coincident with their immigration
into England. The Board of Guardians
of St. George's, Hanover-square, distinctly
affirm that Archbishop MANNING is intro-
ducing " foreigners " to take charge of
one or more "rate-supported schools," and
they call upon the Local Government Board to
see "discontinued forthwith" what, they
undertake to say, "is utterly repugnant to the
feelings of the vast majority •of Englishmen."
In the Catholic school at North Hyde, nearly
five hundred boys are under twelve Brethren .
of the Order of St. Vincent de Paul, all
Belgians. At the same time, the public hears
of a crowded meeting of Roman Catholics at
Islington under the chairmanship of Canon
OAKLEY, formerly of the Church of England,
for the clearly-avowed purpose of advancing
the political as well as the religious interests
.of their denomination, The reverend gentle-
man appears to have explained that the
objects were, a strong organization in every
district of London ; unity of action among the
Catholics of England; to defend the Holy
Father, and show that there are in England a
large number of good Catholics who sympathise
with him, and will aid him according to their
means; to preserve the Catholic religion, and
defend her religious orders in this country;
to encourage Catholic literature in every
form; to see that they were this year put on
the Parliamentary register; to utilise the now
Education Act in the interests of the Catholic
religion; to agitate for the Prison Ministers'
Bill; and to further the temperance move-
ment.

Now, none of us will for a moment question
the perfect right of the Catholics to take care
of themselves, whether politically or religiously.
We must not, however, neglect the signs of
tho times in which we live; nor should those
on whose conduct so much depends, in any
attempt to maintain the balance of public
opinion on the right aide with respect to the
principles and practice of civil and religious
liberty, undervalue the importance of pursu-
ing such a line of conduct between class and
class, as will tend to make and keep the moral
sense and the sober reason of Englishmen
strong for every legitimate purpose of
national co-operation and patriotic self-
defence.

articles.title: HARVEST.
articles.text:
THE HARVEST.

EvEny eye may see that GOD has given us
a good harvest. The best, or, at least, the
least enthusiastic, judges admit the fact. Of
course, we hear of some amount of blight,
mildew, and rust affecting samples and lower-
ing bulk. But, as a whole, the crops are
admitted to be excellent, and to be coming to
rick in good order. At any rate, takins the

•
globe round, there is an ample supply for man
and beast. The storms of July were the
result of a ripening heat, and the rains wore
prevented from doing much harm by intervals
of breeze and dry warmth, The first week
of August was variable in weather; but we
now have a spell of sun and wind without
either sultriness or wet. in fact, the crops
were well-grown, well-matured, and are being
well-garnered. The reaping machines are
effecting a rapid harvest, except in the back-
ward districts. It is to be hoped that pros-
perity will warm the hearts of employers
towards those who sowed and are reaping
the corn.

EDUCATION AND HEATHENISM.
WE have no taste for theological contro-
versy, nor do we think the columns of a news-
paper the most suitable channel for the con-
veyance of argument on disputed dogmas to
the public mind.' But we have had a bit of a
fight this week, not strictly religious, but
bordering thereon, which for its connection
with another interesting subject may, we
think, he very properly noticed:
We should pay very little attention to any-
thing our bishops or archbishops have to say
about heathens or heathenism in London
knowing, as we do, how much of a tendency
there is amongst them to talk conventional old
fashioned nonsense on such subjects. But it
is impossible not to be struck with the candour
and dignity of the rebuke administered by
certain heathen remonstrants in England to
the PRIMATE. for what he has uttered on this
subject. It is said that clergymen sometimes
take liberties with the understandings of their
hearers, because they stand seven or eight
feet above contradiction, How far the LORD
Puntain should stand above, we dare not
venture to say. But, in spite of this, certain
men with almost unpronouucable names, and
no doubt with turbans and loose trousers, fire
off against our archbishop as unceremoniously
as if their trousers and head-gear were of the
most orthodox pattern. 1
They actually charged his lordship with
igoorance, and insinuate that they lean towards
our philosophers rather than in the direction
of our bishops, and that what they have in their
heads as religious thought is as good as any-
thing his grace can give them, An inference
May be drawn from this unfavourable to foreign
missions which we do not care to even hint at
here, but we may be allowed to refer to the
necessity there is for missions much nearer
home, and we may :add , for that most
effectual Qf all missionaries, the schoolmaster,
Who by hie timely action on the child prevents
the growth of ' alhousand hea.thertisms every-
where round about us, which our archbishops,
bishops, rectors, and all other orders of
ministers in the Church find it so difficult to
deal with, so impossible to cure.
Let the Archbishop of CANTERBURY read
the accounts published by oar papers of the
Belfast riots, and tell us what he thinks about
thorn as specimens of heathenism. Men of
the same nation, men with similar interests,
Men whose duty it is to dwell together in
peace, wounding and killing each other, saoking
each other's homes and burning and deStroy-
ing all they eatt lay their hands on. What,
we ask, is the cause of this'? They differ in
religion, and in consequence are trained to
hate each other, are educated separately, live
separately, and seareely over come together
except for the purpose of blackening each
other's eyes, or breaking each other's heads.
We should be sorry to point this out to the
heathens who ' are at the present moment so
hard on the ARCHBISHOP in the columns of the
Times. We BUSpCOt ARDESHEER 13. KAPADAI
might make it an uncomfortable text on which
to preach a sermon on charity, and the need of
Home Missions to the LORD PnumE. But
we think we may draw Mr. GLADSTONE'S and
Mr. FORSTER'S attention to it; a little refleo-
tion on it may be of use to them in framing
the new Irish Education Bill. We have not
much hope in connection with the matter,
but it may suggest the propriety of framing a
system of national education, in which the
school cannot be made into a forcing bed for
the growth of bigotry, and the hatreds and
Violences which grow out of it.
Of course, it is a right thing enough to con-
ciliate the clergy, and to humour pare ntal

prejudices; but when scenes such as those at
Belfast can be enacted—when we see a mag-
nificent country almost paralyzed by the reli-
gious hatreds and strifes of its people, it is
time .to ask ourselves whether it would not be
well for the Government to take courage, and
by making our school education unseetarian,
give religious charity room to grow, leaving
religious teaching to parents and nun of good
heart in the various churches, whose teaching
of religious truth or doctrinal peculiarity will
be tempered, by the affections of life and to
some extent regulated by the requirements of
good neighbourhood. Should this not be done,
we may see, long before SYDNEY SMITH'S Now
Zealander sits on the broken column of
London..bridge, turbaned missionaries from
the East going about our streets for the
purpose of teaching us the duty of loving and
helping each other as the ehildren of a common
father, whose will is that we should dwell
together in peace.

articles.title: PRIME MINISTER OF SPAIN.
articles.text:
THE PRIME MINISTER OF SPAIN.

Wu= the King of SPAIN is gaining golden
opinions among his subjects in every place lie
visits, Senor ZORRILLA. has been making a
speech to a large meeting of electors at
Madrid, the tone and tenor of which are
well calculated to consolidate the Liberal
party. Ho declares his policy to be, to main-
tain and. carry out the individual rights
sanctioned by the Constitution, the conquests
gained by the Revolution. In dealing with the
difficult subject of the priests, he promised them
liberty and independence; but he gave them
notice, that they must be prepared for
measures which will secure to the people full
religious liberty and to public right security
against sacerdotal tampering and ecclesiastical
intrigue. Turning to financial matters, the
seriousness of which ho did not disguise, lie
hoped, nevertheless, for a satisfactory and
early solution of the difficulty. He promised
strict economy ; and, while determined to pro-
mote order, he was careful to observe, that it
did not consist in nor was promoted by meeting
strikes in trade by shots of cannon, but in
respecting the rights of all and in holding all
alike to the obedience or the penalty of law.
With respect to pretenders to the throne, he
seemed to point to the Alphonsists as the
parties most likely to be troublesome, while,
with reference to Cuba and the colonies, he
declared not only for the honour and dignity,
but also for tho integrity of the dominions.
Aocording to letters written about the middle
of -July the insurgents under PEREZ, strongly
posted on their mountain fortresses, , had
repelled the Royalists on every attack'. G-outt.z
also commands in Eastern Cuba, the men in
arms being five thousand in all. Cuba is the
weak point of any Liberal ministry in Spain
that does not go for universal freedom.

articles.title: PRIITARY EDUCATION IN FILANCE.
articles.text:
PRIITARY EDUCATION IN FILANCE.

LIE report of the commission on primary
education is highly unsatisfactory to French
Liberals, who regard it as nothing less than
a bold stroke by the clerical party dealt
against real education, and as an organized
plan for throwing the young entirely into the
hands of the clergy.
The proposed law, says the Corsaire, does
not make education compulsory. It is not
gratuitous, and the first place in it is given
to religious instruction. Finally, with regard
to the choice of the teaching and of the teacher,
there is a Whole combination of interferences
by local councils, and special commissions
wherein the parish priest naturally takes the
lead, and of the vote of parents from which
the best 'results are expected. It is Calculated
that if the priests cannot influence the local
councils, he will at least have weight with the
speeial Commissions Which are instituted to
this effect, and with the parents, who, when
educational cinestiens come On, will vote as the
priest tells them.
By this machinery secular schools will be
replaced by religious schools which will carry
on. a 'furious competition with the former.
by utilizing sermons, visits, and
caluinq,, the lay schoolmasters who refuse to
obey the priests will be diSmissed, to be re-
placed by others entirely sulmiLsiVe to, or
devoted to the interest 4, Of religion if net
through conviction, at least through fear. It

is not ill-done, you see; but where it even
better contrived, it is doubtful whether these
tactics will succeed.

France will not have the positive, utili-
tarian instruction which the people desires,
neither will it have the monkish education it
is proposed to restore. Clericalism may take
children; it will not keep them when they
have reached manhood.

Those who demand compulsory, gratuitous,
and lay education are frank enough to say
why they wish for this. Clericalism, so well re-
presented by the commission, is more cautious
and takes good care not to own its hope and
aim. It attempts to deprive the State of its
power over education, not to emancipate
minds from ministerial regulation, but bemuse
the State is too secular, is not religious
enough, even when the men placed at its
head are animated. by the purest Catholic
zeal.

The State in Prance has always been the
protector and ally of the Church; but that is
not enough, it will be mistress; she will have
the State not for her ally only, but for her
servant; and as the State, though favourable
to the Church, means to divide authority and
government with her; as, after having been
Voltairian under the Monarchy of July, and
somewhat Galilean under the Empire, it be-
came completely indifferent under the Re-
public, and interfere only in public affairs,
and not in those relating to the conscience,
clericalism takes precautions in order to
remain master of the education which secures
its dominion over souls.

What it appeals to, is neither the moral
authority of the Church, nor the antiquity
and legitimacy of its Power, nor the supe-
riority of its doctrine. Not at all. Skilled
in falsehoods, in soptilsms; and in equivocation,
it calls upon liberty. Liberty, mark you!
It is in the name of liberty that BAZILE Speaks,
that ESCOBAIt writes, that FALLOUX legislates;
it is in the name of liberty that Dui,Armour,
Du MEAUX, and LumoNT reply, by an obscu-
rantist law, to the petitions calling for the
organization of education.
What, then, is this liberty which comes
suddenly to enamour the hearts which, but
yesterday, burnt with holy zeal for its impla-
cable enemy authority, divine, pontifical,
royal, administrative and social? The liberty
of parents forsooth! But the question is not
with regard to the parents, but to the
children. The liberty of parents is the
exercise of authority without restraint, or
rule or qualification over beings who can
neither protest nor defend themselves; it
is despotism in the family, as the liberty
of the husband is despotism in the house-
hold, and the liberty of the monarch despotism
in the State.

This is not an occasion for sentiment and
rhetoric. It is all very well to say that
parents love their children and know better
than anyone else what suits them ; that they
are full of tenderness and patience towards
them and of forethought on their behalf;
that their love is the best guarantee for
the accomplishment of their duties and for
the intelligence with which these duties are
accomplished.
Facts and statistics give an eloquent and
'painful denial to these sentimental and
rhetorical assertions of rhetoricians, But,
-granting that all parents without exception
have the same desire to give health, educa-
tion, and comfort to their children, and to
guarantee these to them in future, the desire
is not sufficient, there must also be com-
petency and capacity; and most parents have
not this competency because they aro igno-
rant of the first notions of medicine 'and
of the laws of health, the first elements of
the materials of education, and the first rudi-
ments of economy, art, and industry.
If our follow-citizens had all, received the
instruction which should be that of a man Of
the 19th century, there might be some reason
to speak of the liberty of the initiative of 'the
parents, because these could judge of the
education given to their children, and because
they could educate thorn themselves. But
that parents might exercise the liberty claimed
on their behalf, they should not be submitted
to the dominion of those two soeittl fatalities
—ignorance and wretchedness.

It is not, indeed, pleasant to ace the State
interfere in everything, and especially in those
wherein the individual should act freely. But
if there be a case in which the authority of
the State appears legitimate, it is in that of
the protection and education of children.
Children do not belong to their parents, as
the clerical commission seems to believe, as
Catholic doctrine proclaims, and as too madY
think. They belong to themselves; they are
persons in course of formation, they are not
things, the property of those who bre-tight
them into the world, but beings who will one
day be men, citizens, and who bring with them
at their birthrights which all, even: their
parents, are bound to respect. The State is to
them a guardian, having the mission of
protecting their persons and those rights whieh
they are, as yet, incapable of defending ; who,
then, can protect their liberty, their interests,
and their future, against the egotistical or
capricious tyranny of parents if not the State,
or, at least, collective authority ?
Our barbarous civilization gives a father
the right of depriving his child of all Elite 9,.
tion, of striking him, of humiliating him. Of
sacrificing him to a caprice, to a mania, .and/
provided there are no serious wounds, or no
peculiar severity of imprisonment, no one
interferes to protect this poor young being
condemned from infancy, and who will,
throughout his life, retain the painful recollec-
tion of the early years during which he was
devoted to ignorance, disgust, and despair.
It is necessary, out of respect to humanity,
to interfere, and, having cared for the protec-
tion of animals, to think a little about protect-
ing children, securing their freedom against
paternal tyranny, and their Conscience against
the falsehoods of the clergy, and teaching them
that self-respect without which there is neither
settled society nor a free people.

articles.title: JOTTINGS OF A DEPUTATION TO LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
JOTTINGS OF A DEPUTATION TO
LANCASHIRE.

We arrive at Ashton in a heavy thunderstorm,
and seek shelter in the nearest " public " or
"vault," as it is called in this part. There must be
a close sympathy between this part of the country
and the clouds for they seem to be on very intimate
terms. Our ingenious cousins in America, who
recently in the extremity of their wits, discharged
a heavy battery at the clouds, and by the concus-
sion of the air brought down a generous shower,
would have no occupation here, for it rains so un-
mercifully in Lancashire that only a few weeks since
the Medlock rose some eighteen feet through
heavy rains and drainage fromthe Derbyshire and
aurrounding hills that not only was great destruc-
tion to life and property -the result, but dead
bodies were even washed out of their graves and
floated down the stroets of Manchester.

But while the rain is pouring, we find that the
apartment to which we are driven by stress of
weather, possesses some objects of interest. A
prominent announcement informs us that the
"Ashton and D uckerfleld Entomological Society"
holds its monthly meetings here. We soon dis-
cover ample evidence that there is no lack of
activity in the members of this society between
meeting nights, for they have caught more butter-
flies than one would think it were possible to
catch in a generation, and very artistic use has
been made of them; all sorts of designs, emblems,
pictures, and hieroglyphics have been constructed
of butterflies of all sizes and colours. Its transi-
tion states from moth, Chrysalis, and fly is also
illustrated by numberless specimens in a case to
themselves. A curious fact is related to us con-
cerning the method of catching butterflies. There
is a peculiarity about one kind, that when it is
emerging from the chrysalis state, if taken, say to
an open field and placed under a net, it has the
property of attracting butterflies for miles around;
but if, by any accident, a connection is formed
between it and any of its visitors, this power of
attraction instantly ceases, and, all its would-be
friends diaappear and return no more.
Much of the leisure time of workmen in various
parts of Lancashire i spent in these entomological
and also in botanical pursuits, and microscopical
instruments of very powerful and expensive kinds
are frequently met with in their homes, by the
use of which they are enabled to partake of the
instruction and pleasures afforded by the most
bewitching of sciences. The heavy rain has now
driven other company into our midst, and at a side
table a party—not a scientific one—have resolved
upon a small concert, and one of their number is
ust about to open the ball. Mr. Dickens has well
described the great tendency of amateur singers to
ffx their eyes upon the ceiling and the gesticula-
tions and apologies which preeede the absorbing
effort. Our friend hero is not troubled with any
delicacy of that kind, for not a limb nor muscle
moves, and for any outward and visible sign he
might be exaMining the peculiarities of the table
top.

But the rain is over now, and as we have not
come here to spend our time and money for our
own amusement, we wait upon the nearest aeon-

tory to solicit his co-operation towards a public
meeting. We find that while holding the position
of secretary to a trade society, he is also foreman
of a considerable firm where he works; moreover,
that his employer is the respected treasarer of the
same society, an office which he highly values.
This circumstance is instructive, as showing the
relations existing between employers and em-
ployed in Lancashire. Every town we visit we
find evidence of a far better understanding pre-
vailing on the knotty questions of capital and
labour, and it is only fair to assume that this is to
a great extent owing to the mutual agreements
entered into between the two parties directly in-
terested. Codes of working rules arc established
in all Lancashire towns as a matter of course, by
• which the hours of labour, wages, and all
other terms and conditions under Which labour
shall be bought and sold, are fully and fairly set
forth, and signed by responsible parties on behalf
of workmen and masters. Of the various forms of
arbitration, this is one which is the most
sensible and effectual, and the more towns
we visit the firmer becomes our con-
viction that the workmen of London never made
a wiser demand than that a code of working rules
eh tild in future be mutually agreed upon, defin-
ing their wages, hours of labour, etc. Indirectly,
this is the surest mode of preventing strikes and
difficulties, for, when the process of giving notice
of alterations through the machinery always pro-
vided by a code of rules, has to be complied with,
a better deliberation and a calmer appeal to reason
is the result which seldom fails to lead to a
friendly arrangement of the matter in dispute.
Apropos of arbitration, we had subsequently the
privilege of attending a private meeting of the
joiners of a large town, called for the purpose of
deciding the proPriety of giving notice' of altera-
tions in time and wages. There was this
peculiarity in the working rules of this town,
that a gentleman of high reputation possessing
no confidence of masters and meu is appointed to
settle all disputes that may arise, and it was
curious to notice the speculative tendency of the
meeting in view of this fact. As the discussion
went on the actual requirements of the men
appeared to be a rise of wages of 2s. per week ;
but as the process of obtaining had to be taken
into consideration, it was ultimately resolved to
ask the employers for 3s. per week and 2-1 hours
reduction in time.

Leaving my readers to draw their own in-
ferences from this, I must reserve somo remarks
On the Tirade UllloeiSel of Lancashire for next
week.

articles.title: METROPOLITAN WORKMEN'S CLUBS,
articles.text:
METROPOLITAN WORKMEN'S CLUBS,

The Working Men's Club and Institute
Union had on Monday its annual extursion.
Between one and two thousand men, women,
and children were conveyed in special trains
to Knob ° Park, Sevenoaks, the seat of Lord
Bnckhurst. The weather was fine, and the ex-
cursionists wore even more genial than the
weather, They had some eight or nine hours
of merrymaking, and they returned to town
by the seven o'clock train. Once a year as
many members of the affiliated societies as
can he got together pay a visit to some noble-
man or gentleman who offers them the use of
his grounds. They prefer parks to public re-
creation grounds on principle, one great ob-
ject of the promoters of the movement being
to inorease the good fellowship between classes
by the sense of civilities and courtesies offered
and received. In previous years the excur-
sionists have called in their thousands" at
the homes of Lord Salisbury and Lord Ports-
mouth; this year, as has been stated, they
went to Snole. dis lordship was not there to
see them; and his house was closed. But they
saw some very beautiful scenery, and in spite
of a printed prohibition against" loitering
about or stopping on:the green sward in front
of Knob-house," they contrived to obtain
furtive views of a noble old mansion that may
be said to belong to the history of their
country.
The excursion took place under the super-
vision of the committee of the Club and
Institute Union. A 30 miles' ride by rail
without stoppages, at a good pace, through the
rich and undulating scenery of Kent, is of
itself a thing to be enjoyed; but pleasant and
jovial company was added to the enjoyments
of that short and rapid journey. Two bands
from London—one attired in the uniform of
the Queen's Westminster Volunteers, and the
other in the less showy undress of the L divi.
sion of the police—mustered in the station.
yard, and the excursionists marched off at a
brisk pace through the old-fashioned town of
Sevenoaks to Kook-house. The romantio
park, which was kindly thrown open by Lord
Buckhurst to the Londoners, is "justly cele-
brated for its extent, beauty, and variety of
scenery." It is full of noble trees, shady
avenues, picturesque mounds, and open glades,
with wildernesses of furze and fields of bracken,
while in a most commanding position stands
the stately pile, produced by the genius of

several generations of architects, and the home
of a long line of powerful magnates—Knolo
House, the delight and glory of the archmo-
logists of Kent. The building covers several
acres, and consists, as it were,
•of many
mansions blended into one harmonious
whole, each section being a distinct speci-
men of a particular style of architecture.
The holiday folk lost no opportunity of enjoy-
ing themselves. A team of enthusiastic
cricketers pitched their stumps and commenced
play; others worried a tough-looking foot-
ball; races ani jumping matches occupied the
attention of some; while dancing, " kiss in
the ring," and other open-air amusements
were equally attractive to many. The mere
fact of being able to sit on the grass in the
grateful shade of some majestic tree, breathing
the balmy air and watching the active enjoy-
ments of their companions, proved sufficient
entertainment for not an inconsiderable por-
tion of the party, while a few wandered "up
hill and down dale" all over the park, dis-
covering new phases in the scenery, and now
and again just catching a glimpse of the fleer
as they gambolled and fed in the distance.
Abundance of refreshments were provided at
moderate charges, and everything was arranged
to make the excursion thoroughly successful.
One little hitch, however, occurred at the end
of the day, which caused much grumbling and
some inconvenience—the return train went off
with but half its freight, and the executive,
the bands, and several hundred people were
lisft behind to get to London as best they could
by the later trains. However, "alt's well
that ends well," and the excursionists were
finally deposited safely at Charing-eross, tired
and weary, at an hour before midnight.

articles.title: -FORESTERS AT THE CRYSTAL PALACE.
articles.text:
THE -FORESTERS AT THE CRYSTAL
PALACE.

The officers and members of this largo and
influential order had their usual annual
gatherilig On Tuesday last at the "palace of
the pkiplb.'''.-The weather was all that could
be wiithea:- here was just wind enough to
maid wtstio -d cool, and the sight of the
hut onelliaTO a that assembled to see Blondin
ti
wits Somethingato remember. In 1869, 03,000;
in 1870;.d3,000 ; in 1871, 84,000 assembled
in the Palace ; and it was the silent hope of
the directors' and no doubt of the shareholders,
also that the total of 100,000 might have been
recorded for '72. Fortune has willed it other-
wise. There were not more that 70,000—a
mere trifle—to wateh the celebrated Freuch-
man go through his performances. Seventy
thousand upturned faces following the slightest
motion of one man, would make many a one
feel nervous • but M. Blondin has steed this
public gaze for many years, and it is needless
to say that he flinched not on this occasion.
Dancing on the green, the pastime of the
good old Englishman, was immediately com-
menced with great energy, and not until
darkness made a distinction between partners
somewhat difficult were the bands brought to
silence. Among all the amusements, how-
ever, there• was nothing that caused
such genuine and , prolonged enjoyment as
the sports upon the lake. A pole
some thirty feet long is put out at
about six feet from the water. At the end is
a square wicker-work basket attached with a
rope to the end of the pole, in suoh a manner
that only he whJ reaches the pole by walking
on it can unloosen the rope and open the con-
tents—a live pig. Some men made very
laudable and earnest endeavours to keep in an
upright position, but had to give it up for a
bad job, and jump for safety into the water.
The pig, after once or twice subjected to an
involuntary bath, seemed to have had enough of
it, for it escaped. Being provided with a fair
quantity of fat bacon it swam excellently
and soon out-distanced its pursuers. The
boat containing the St. Oeorge's Rifle band—
who were performing on the water—became a
momentary harbour of- refuge; but when the
claimants stormed the boat on all sides the
squealing fugitive obtained a fair 'chance hy
being hurled into the midst of the lake, where,
grunting for very life, it was caught by one
fortunate individual, and carried ashore in
triumph. There were several boat-races,
canoe-races, and swimming snatches, all of
which attracted• much attention. Mr. Beek=
with, with his two sons and daughter of eight,
went through some very clever performances.
The total number of visitors during the day
amounted to 84,950, the largest by twenty-
five that has ever been known on Foresters'
day. The crush occasionally was, of course,
very great. When a move was made up the
principal staircase progress was tediously
slow, but otherwise there was sanely any
inconvenience. There was very little drunk-
enness, and the 206 and odd policemen who
were on duty did not seem by any means
overworked. Outside the building the sight
was almost equally interesting. The entire
neighbourh6od swarmed with holiday makers.
Every spare horse • in the metropolis had
apparently been pressed into duty, and the
number of wheelbarrows on which light re-
freshments were displayed for sale was some-
thing amazing. It was a thorough day for
the people, and it is much to the credit of the
Ancient Order of Foresters that such an enor-
mous mass of people should have behaved in
every respect with propriety. '

MR. WALTER MORRISON, M.P., ON

articles.title: AGRICULT URAL •CO-OPERATION.
articles.text:
AGRICULT URAL •CO-OPERATION.

•
At the annual meting of the Agricultural
and Horticultural Association, recently held
at Cardiff, Mr. Waltcr Morrison, M.P.,
made the following appr.vriate speech. He
said :--

lie supposed he might take that day's attend-
ance as au evidence, that the growth of the Asso-
ciation in numbers, power, and influence, was
accompanied by a growth among them of the
co-Operative spirit; that all felt more Strongly each
year that the work of combating fraud and
adulteration by means of co-operation was the
personal concern of • each member' and that in
future they might Count upon that living interest
without which no society could 'achieve a success
and with which no .society could ever fail. The
fifth year, of the Assotiation'a existence had been-a
remarkable one. During . the past spring the
business had taken such a march forward as
evidenced an awakening of the public mind to
, their movement. On doe whole. year there was an
increase, and if they compared. the rate of the
progrees, viz., 57 per cent., with the 35 per cent.
increase of the previous year, and the 16 per cent.
increase Of the year before that, they would See
how great a probable future lay' before the Agri-
cultural and Horticultural Association. The
sales in the 'fifth year were, in fact, just' five
Ulnas as large as the sales in the first year.

The proportion of expenses to business was a
crucial test of the management of co-operatiTe
societies. The one thousand co-operative societies
which the working men of Lancashire Yorkshire,
and other industrial, centres had established to
economise their household expenditure, were well
known to be con'cltict,:d with an ability, economy,
and close attention to the details of expenditure
unparalleled in ordinary trading concerns. They
might, therefore, be flirty taken as a high stan-
dard to compare with as regards the percentage
of expenses. Well, the Government return which
was last year granted upon his (Mr. Morrison's) i
motion n the House of Commons, showed the
average Working expenses of these societies to be
about 41 per cent. upon their sales. no expenses
of the Agricultural Association, inclusive of
• management, wore under 4 per cent., and were
gradually becoming proportionately lighter as the
business grow. He believed the best managed of
other London societies—the Civil Service ASElOCift-
tiono—found their expenses reach nearly 6 per
cent. upon their sales; and this fact of the greater
expensiveness of operations in London than in the
country brought the economical ,administration of
the Agricultural Association into yet greater ro.
lief.

The report of the-Council had touched upon
the question of adulteration. That questioa was
in fact at once the most important and the most
diffieult they had to deal with. The report showed
that even the inannres of the most respectable
houses were found, upon analysis, to contain from
20s. to 80s. per ton less fertilising strength thaa
those which an association of agriculturists like
theirs, buying for home consumption, would
naturally purchase. Hero was a difference of 20
to 26 per cent. saving In value. But this wits a
trifle compared to the revelations which from time
to time ewe before tbe COullai or manures and
feeding stuffs, and seeds, sold all over England by
unscrupulous merchants, through ignorant agents,
whom they tempted to push their igoodifor the
sake of large commissions. Iti one case, an
ordinary superphosphate of lime of 'loss strength
than they were supplying to thtir members at £4
per ton, was being advertised as highly con-
centrated manure at £9 per ton. In another
instance a manure was being pushed in the
southern and midland counties at £8 per ton,
which contained only. 8 per cent. of soluble
phosphate, Three tons or 418 pound worth of
this precious compound would therefore be required
to equal in real valua L 4 of the Association's
superphosphate. And within ,the last two months
the Association had discovered, not far frorn their
own wharf, a manufactory of adulterated manures
where common superphosphate was being mixed
with tan refuse and, other Avesta materials, for
sale, under a good-sounding title, at far more than
twice its proper value. These were only a few
of the cases which came before the Council, and
which kept over before them the greatneAs of the
evil they had to conquer. If every member of
the Association could see these things as they (tho
Council) saw theta, he honeyed they would feel A
new sense of the value of the Association, and
new earnestness in the came of agricultural co-
operation.

Mr. Morrison, after referring to the establishment
of the Agricultural Economist, and pointiag out
its convenience and value as an organ for inter-
change of opinion between the members, proceeded
to speak of the new arrangements for seed supply,
and congratulated the Association upon having
been able at length to take this department out of
the hands of contractors and establish a warehouse
of their own. They would now be able to test
their stocks of seeds as they did their stocks of
manures, and make sure of the tpiality of what
they bought. They proposed to make special
efforts to supply co-operative societies with their
tested seeds, and especially 'working meals societies
with genuine flower and vegetable seeds for the
small garden plots and allotments which were so
desirable an addition to the home of every work.
ing man and labourer. Mr. Morrison concluded
by moving the adoption of the report.

Good value for money is desired by all, but with
articles that cannot be judged of by appearance';
careful purehasQrs rely on the high standing of
