articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Next year's meeting of the British Assooia-
tion is to be held at Bradford, and the gather-
ing of 1874 at Belfast. Dr. James Prescott
Joule is the !law president.

The August sessions of the Central Criminal
Court were opened on Monday, wheu there
were 101 prisoners for trial. Thomas Edwards,
the second of the witnesses in the Partinston
divorce suit, who had been indicted for perjury,
was convicted, and sentenced to eighteen
mouths' imprisonment with hard labour.
Three men were found guilty of conspiracy to
obtain 330 tons of coal by false pretences,
and each of them was ordered to undergo
five years' penal servitude. William Barron,
68, for the possession of t oining implements,
was sentenced to be kept in penal servitude
for 15 years.

The convict Charles Field, who was con-
demned to death at the Chester Assizes for the
murder of his wife, has been pronounced
insane, and the capital sentence will not,
therefore, be carried out.

A street preacher named Gibson was on
Monday charged at the Lambeth Police-
court with having created an obstruotion in a
public thoroughfare by assembling a crowd to
listen to his utteranoes. He had been pre-
viously cautioned by the police, and was now
ordered to enter into his recognisances in the
sum of £lO to keep the peace.

• The stringent provisions of. the Lioensing
Act for the punishment of drunkenness are
now generally enforced in London. At Mary-
lebone, on Monday, an offender who had been
guilty of disorderly conduct, while in a state
of intoxication, was sentenced to seven
days' hard labour without the option of a
fine,

Another charge of baby-farming was in-
vestigated on Monday. Jane Haley, about 50
years of age, was brought up on an accusation
of having ill-treated three children entrusted
to her care, by neglecting to provide them
with proper food and clothing. The prisoner,
who was remanded, would have been roughly
treated. by an. assembled crowd had not the
police interfered.

From New York we hear that Judge Bar-
nard has been removed from the bench by a.
unanimous vote of the Court. He is diseitiali-
fled for holding office in future, and found
guilty on all the charges connected with the
Erie Itailway suits instituted by the English
shareholders.

A telegram from Washington attributes to
the Secretary of the British-American Com-
mission at Geneva the statement that twenty
eases of compensation under the Washington
Treaty have been already settled, and that
less than three per cent, of the amounts
claimed have been awarded. It is added that
a large number of eases await the September
session. Monday's sitting of the Arbitration
Court lasted from noon till half-past four? and
VMS devoted to the reading of the printed
pleadings. Sir Round°ll Palmer was not pre-
sent. Communications respecting the results
of the sittings will, it is expected, be made
shortly.

Assaults upon the police continue to occupy
a considerable share of the metropolitan
magistrates' attention. At Westminster
William Campbell, a labourer, has been con-
victed of beating Constable 231 B, and a
sentence of four months' imprisonment with
hard labour was passed. At Clerken.well
there were four cases of this description, in
two of which the offenders received three
months' Imprisonment; in the third a fine of
25e. Was Inflicted; and in the fourth the
defendant was remanded. At Marlborough-
street, John Dalton, a tailor, was brought up
on a charge of having stabbed a constable, and
was remanded for inquiries. At Southwark,
James Kirby, who had violently assailed a
policeman, was sent to prison for six months.
Two women, named Fitzgerald and Wallace,
who had aided Kirby, were allotted three and
two months of the like punishment.

Apprehensions are, it is alleged, entertained
at 3ladrid of a fresh Carlist outbreak, joined
by the partisans of the ex-Queen Isabella.

General Uhrich, the Governor of Strasburg
during the memorable siege, is on the point of
Issuing at Paris an elaborate " Apology. " for
his conduct at that trying period, the title of
it being "Documents relating to the Siege of
Strasburg." The prohibition of any publics-
cation of this kind having ceased on his retire-
ment from the army, after fifty years'
service, the general enters very fully into
the question of the surrender of the fortress,
and of the impeachment of his own honour in
connection with that event, with the same
vigour which he displayed against the German
bombardment, and denounces his detractors
in indignant terms,

,T.

Attention was called, at a coroner's inquest
which was held on Saturday, to the number,of
children who are drowned through falling
into the water at Whitehall•stairs. According
to a juryman, if a returu could be obtained of
the numerous deaths which occurred there,
the public would be amazel. The coroner
undertook to bring the matter before the
Boark of Works.

The Universal Exhibition to be held next
year at Vienna, will manifestly be on a very
grand scale. It will occupy an area of four
or live English square miles, and the covered
space will considerably exceed that of the
monster Paris Exhibition of 1867. A rotunda
will rise from the centre of the building, and
be the largest canopy-shaped edifice without
supports that has ever been erected. There
will be a separate hall for machinery in motion
890 metres in length and 28 in width. The
site of the building is described as being the
heart of a park unsurpassed for beauty by any
in Europe.

A Paris Correspondent gives a singular
narrative of the degradation of Captain
Cerfbeer for desertion to the Germans. The
chief interest in the story lies in the fact that,
after being subjected to ignominious depriva-
tion of his rank of officer and declared
unworthy to serve his country, the ex-captain
will, so far as the future is concerned, only
ba compelled, at the worst, to live for ten
years on a fine estate which he possesses in
Lorraine. This mild penalty is a mitigation
by M. Thiers of the sentence of death pro •
nouneed by a court-martial.

M. Thiers paid a visit on Saturday afternoon,
with Madame Thiel", to Honfleur. The Pre
feet of the Department of Calvados, the Mayor
of Honfleur, and the President of the Chamber
of Commerce, went along the road to Trouville
to meet him, but failed to do so in conse-
quence of his taking a cross road. On
alighting at the Hotel de Ville he was
received by the sub-prefect. The town and
port were gaily decorated with flags in honour
of the illustrious visitor; and M. Thiers
appears to have spent a considerable time in
examining a project for the construction of a
large basin to prevent the accumulation of
sand in the harbour, and for the extension of
the jetty. On returning to the HOWL de Ville
he was loudly cheered.

From a telegram from Mexieo, received in
New York, it appears that the rebellion has
come to an end. All the leaders have, it is
stated, either submitted or been captured..

The Tichborne me was the, subject of
another polioe-court application on Tuesday,
when Mr. Abraham Anidjah asked the Bow
-
street magistrate for a 'summons against Mr.
Guildford. Onslow, M.P., for an alleged libel
contained in a letter addressed by the hon.
gentleman to an evening contemporary. A.
communication which he had addressed to tho
newspaper in question, contradicting the
statements made by Mr. Onslow, had not been
inserted. The summons was granted,

On Tuesday the Marlborough - street
police magistrate sent to prison for four
months one Henry Moore, for an assault upon
his wife. At Worship-street a man named
Frank Perry received six months' bard labour
for a similar offence.

The Bien Public, alluding to the rumour
persistently repeated by some Paris journals,
that the .Freneh. Government contemplate
authorising experimentally gambling-houses
at Engbien, Vichy, Aix, Pau, and 'other
places, alarms authoritatively that it ever has
refused, and ever will refuse to listen to any
proposition of that kind. refuse,
may be
its needs, an honest Government, it is added,
seems to seek revenue from immorality and
vice, and the partisans of gaming-tables may
rest assured that they will not be revived
either partially or generally.

According to a telegram received from a
correspondent, the visit of M. Thiers to Havre
is again postponed On account of pressing and
prior engagements. Military manceuvres on
a large scale in France were said to have been
resolved upon by the President and the
Minister of War, though it is not stated
whether they will occur at the same time as
those which the Prussians propose to hold in
the occupied pro'vinces.

Not less than £3,800,000, according to the
Patrie, is the figure representing the decline
of the French revenue from indirect taxation
during the first half of 1872,

The Japanese EnAassy, after dining with
Lard Granville, visited the litternational
Exhibition on Monday, and were shown the
principal objects of interest by his lordship.
A distinguished company was present.

Attached to the text of the French law on
raw materials, published by the Journal
(*del, is a decree of M. Thiers that certain
clauses applying to a number of natural pro-
ducts shall come into operation immediately.

On Monday evening the Princess of Wales
left Cowes in the Victoria and Albert yacht
for Copenhagen.

Disorders are reported to have broken out
at a bull-fight at Pampeluna, where the band.
played Garibaldi's hymn, and the Carlist sym-
pathisers in the audience tried to stop it. A.
regular "scrimmage "with sticks ensued, in
which the Mayor suffered both indignity and
injury in his attempts to stop the fight, And
the same functionary was afterwards shot at
in the street by Carlists, who were captured.
This story, told in letters received at Bayonne,
fits in so far with the statement from Madrid
that a new insurrection is apprehended, in
which the Carlists and Isabellists will make
common cause.

On Sunday night a serious collision occurred
at the Kew Bridge Station of the North
London Railway, by which many persons
were more or less injured and great damage
done to the rolling stook of the line.

The Thames Regatta was brought to a con-
clusion on Monday, the Champion Fours
being won by the Hammersmith crew after a
magnificent race with the Newcastle men. In
the final heat for the Champion Pair, however,
matters wore reversed, the Tynesiders, (Taylor
and Winship) beating tho Hammersmith re-
presentatives (Thomas and Billie). Fouls
occurred in both races without, however,
interfering with the result.

Arriving on Saturday at Ferrol, King
Amadeus was saluted by the Spanish and
English war-ships in the roads, and most
cordially received, even by the clergy, who
sang "To Deum." Prince Humbert is to
visit his Royal brother after the Italian army
manoeuvres at Somma.

An applioation has been made by Mr. Harry
Boleno, landlord of Old Drury Tavern, for
permission to keep his house open until one
o'clock, on the ground of its contiguity to
Drury-lane Theatre ; but Mr. Flowers stated
that the application should be made, not to a
magistrate, but at Scotland Yard.

The finding and sentence of the general
court martial which was recently engaged in
the trial of Captain Edward O'Donovan
Powell, Royal Marines, were promulgated at
the divisional head-quarters on Monday morn-
ing. The court acquitted the accused on the
more serious charge of drunkenness when in
command of a detachment on the line of march
from Chatham to Gravesend, but found him
guilty of handing over -the command of a
detachment of which he was in ()barge on a
subsequent day to a subaltern, the court sen-
tencing him to be severely reprimanded.

Midhat Pasha has inaugurated his Vizier-
ship with a most promising and thoroughly
European measure in sanctioning the opening
of about 120 miles of railway in the provinoe
of Ronnielia—thus nearly doubling the extent
of working lines in Turkey.

At Blandrord the camp has b3en got into
working order, and oa Tuesday some impor-
tant instruction was given to the troops assem-
bled. Both infantry and cavalry had several
hours of outpost drill, the Guards particularly
distinguishinc, themselves. From preparations
which have been made, it app3ars that during
the next fortnight, until the mancouvres
actually take place, the brigade battalion drill
by the Southern Army will be carried on with
but little cessation. The troops are in excel-
lent health, and. the militia regiments are con-
sidered exceptionally at for duty.

Confession is made by the Gazette des
Tribunaux—in denying an. assertion as to
" numerous " arrests of Communists in Paris
—that such arrests do continue to be made;
and a still uglier fact is added, that more
assaults and insults than ever are offered to
soldiers of the Parisian garrison. Officially,
this is attributed to the return of released
Communists; but the protracted and cause-
less humiliation of Paris by martial law and
the absence of the Government cannot but
have its share in provoking to the offences in
question.

Sir H. Former Hesketh, Bart., died on
Tuesday, at the age of 47. The deceased,
who has filled the offices of Colonel of the
Duke of Lancaster's Militia, Colonel of the
9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers,_ and High
Sheriff of that county, was elected one of the
members for Preston in March, 1862, on the
temporary retirement from the House of Mr.
Asshoton Cross, now one of the representatives
of South-West Lancashire. He was again
returned at the general eleetions of 1865 and
1868, in, the last-mentioned ease after a con-
test in which Lord Edward Howard (the
present Lord Howard of Glossop) was one of
the unsuccessful candidates.

Mr. Cardwell, accompanied by Sir Henry
Storks and Mr. Glyn, on Saturday paid a visit
to the encampment to be occupied by the
southern army in the forthcoming autumn
mancoures.

The majority of the public-houses at Porti-
mouth are now closed at eleven on week dap,
and at ten on Sunday; and the police Atte
that the town has never before been so quiet
during the night.

A. new steam yacht, built for the Empe.ror
of Austria, arrived at Ityde on Sunday evening
en route to the Mediterranean.

On Monday morning Mary Minns, the wife
of a labourer at Walpole St. Andrews, near
Wisbeaeh, and Sarah Ann Minns, bet,
daughter, aged 16, a servant in the employ of
Mr. W. Boon, a farmer, were charged with
the murder of the infant child of the younger
prisoner. The child was born on the 12th
inst., when the mother remained all night at
Mr. Boon's house. The medical evidence was
to the effect that the child was born alive, and
that there were marks of four finger-nails on
one side of the throat and one large nail-mark
on the other, and. an examination presented
evidence of pressure. The girl, on being asked
whether she lived with Mr. Boon, declined to
answer. The coroner's inquest having been
adjourned, the prisoners were apprehended and
brought before the magistrates on Monday,
and they were remanded for a week, bail being
refused.

A shocking accident has happened at Erith.
Thomas Hughes, lighterman of Leamington
-
terrace, Victoria Docks, left home with his
family and friends on Sunday night fort a
moonlight row on the river. When off EMI'
the boat capsized. Five were drowned and
three rescued in an exhausted state. Hughes
having his shoulder dislocated was sent to
Guy's Hospital. The five persons drowned
were Elizabeth Ann Hughes, the wife; Amelia
Hughes daughter, aged, 20; Thomas Hughes,
ton, aged 8; Edward Johnstone, aged 17; and
a young man named George.

It is announced that the Queen,• in the
course of her drives through Edinburgh and
the neighbourhood, has been extremely grati-
fied by the warm and loyal reception which
has been given to her Majesty by all
classes.

The Electoral Reform Association has issued
a circular giving some telling instances of the
inequalities in our present system of represen-
tation, and showing how important measures
may be lost in consequence. On the Mines
Regulation Bill Mr. Staveley Hill moved to
weaken the clause affecting the employment
of miners' children; he was victorious by 13,
but in a minority of 50,000 voters. Again, the
Birmingham Sewage Bill was defeated by the
narrow majoriy of 3, but the 145 who voted
against Sir R. Peel represented 400,000 more
voters than the 148 who enabled him to win
his motion.

A minute has been issued from the Board
of Trade, embodying a number of regulations
relating to the water supply of the metropolis,
under the Act passed in the session of 1871.
These point to a more efficient system of com-
munication pipes, and amongst other pro-
visions it is laid down that no pipe in cows
neotion with the company's water shall, in any
way, communicate with any cistern intended,
for the reception of rain-water.

There are some interesting statistics in the
annual report of the Metropolitan Police Com-
missioners. During the year 1871 there were
added to the duties of the force the supervision
of 226 new streets and two ' squares, a total
length of more than 38 miles, During the
past ten years there were built in the
metropolitan police district nearly 150,000
houses, with an additional length of streets
amounting to 633 miles, equal to the distance
from London to Inverness, and 40 miles
beyond. The conduct of the force during laat
year was highly satisfaotory, for only 14 meo
out of a daily average of 9,700 were charged
before magistrates, and of these four were
acquitted.

Last week a series of experiments was carried
out at Woolwich with the English Galli*
gun, the only mitrailleuse yet introduced into
the service. It is believed that the use of these
weapons will be restricted to boats and
fortresses, where the length and breadth of
the space to be swept lies within comparatively
narrow limits.

At the half-yearly meeting of the Great
Northern Railway Company, on Saturday,,
Colonel Duraiombe, M.P., alluded to the e%;
periment of conveying third-class traffic by all
trains. A million more of this class of pas-
sengers had been carried during the
mouths, as compared with the corresponding
peril:a of 1871, and the result to the revenue
was "rather favourable than otherwise."

The Free Sunday Society has passed
resolution calling upon all the trades and
friendly societies and p organizations
of the metropolis to unite for a great de-
monstratioa in favour of the opeuivg
the national museums to the workiug; elasko4
on Sunday.

On Tuesday the Emperor and Empress of
the French took their departure from
Brighton for the Isle of Wight.

A. Paris correspondent remarks on the fact
that M. Thiers pays the usual penalty of
greatness by being pestered with lunatics of
various kinds. Among these a man named
Jacques Brouillet, to whom belongs the sou-
briquet of the " Fou de Trouville," has
obtained the distinction of being arrested
when inquiring for M. Thiers at the Paris
Prefecture on the pretext that he had an im-
portant communication to make, a sword,
encased in a common-looking stick, having
been found in his possession. M. Thiers likes
Trouville so much that his stay will probably
be extended beyond what was originally in-
tended, but this will not prevent a short
interim visit to Fontainebleau.

Among the -intelligence from the Cape,
extending up to the 23rd of July, is the state-
ment that the dispute with ,the Free State
about the ownership of the diamond fields was
to be settled by arbitration, an agreement
having been come to by Sir H. Barkly and
President Brand as to the conditions. A
survey for a railway from East London to
Queen's Town had been authorised.

Several cruses were disposed of at Tuesday's
sitting of the Central Criminal Court. There
were charges of theft against two letter-
sorters in the employment of the Post-office.
One of the prisoners, a youth of sixteen,
pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to eighteen
months' hard labour. The second, who was
ten years older, was ordered to be kept in
penal servitude for five years. The other
indictments were chiefly for obtaining money
under false pretences, uttering forged. orders,
and offences of a similar description.

Mr. F. Strange, formerly of the Alhambra
Palace, and now of the Royal Surrey Gardens,
having presented a petition for liquidation, a
receiver to the estate has been appointed. The
liabilities are returned at about 4,30,000.

Deaths from starvation in London continue
to be reported. Inquests were on Tuesday
held upon the bodies of a woman fifty two
years of age and a eh ild six months old, and
in both eases death was attributed to want of
food.

The Ramsgate Royal Harbour Regatta
(open to the coast) took place on Tuesday.
The principal race was that between yachts
not exceeding ten tons. Many rowing matches
took place at the same time, though the high
wind that blew all day was hardly favourable
to this class of contests.

From April Ist to the 17th inst. the Ex-
chequer receipts amounted to £26,170,184 as
comparca with £24,209,815 in the corres-
ponding period or last year. The expenditure
has been £28,807,186. On Saturday last the
balance in the Bank of Engkand was
£4,136,424.

The riots in Exeter over the early-closing
provisions of the Licensing Act have not de-
terred the magistrates from their resolve
strictly to adhere to the terms of the new
statute. Summonses have been issued against
seven persons who took a leading part in the
disturban.oea of Monday night.

At tlie Middlesex Sessions Mr. Smythe,
Bandmaster of the Royal Artillery, was
charged with assaulting an inspector of the
South-Eastern Railway at the Charing-cross
Station. The defendant and his band came to
the station at a late hour on a night when they
had been playing at Lord Granville's, expect-
ing. to find a special train to convey them to
Woolwich, and, this not being forthcoming, an
altercation ensued, and Mr. Smythe technically
assaulted the inspector. By arrangement a
verdict of guilty was taken, the defendant
entering into an undertaking to appear for
judgment if called upon.

A young man has been charged at Lambetit
Police Court for abducting a gitl of 15; but
though he was remanded, the evidence against
him was slight, the girl having been found at
the house of a friend.

On Tuesday Mr. Justice Hannen terminated
his sittings in Chombers, and will be succeeded
on Friday by Mr. Justice Quain, the regular
Vacation Judge.

Local, rather than political considerations,
as was generally anticipated, governed the
French Councils- Qpneral in electing their
Presidents and other officials. In the Oise
the Due d'Aumale has been chosen.

Lord Lyons has left Paris for London.

The harvest is now general throughout the
country, the 4ne weather, which seems now to
have set in, and the recent moonlight enabling
the harvestmen to get in the corn with
unusual rapidity. The reports we receive
both as to the quality and quantity of the
grain are very gratifying:

The proposed alterations in the Anglo-
French Commercial Treaty are stated to be
the subject of constant communication be-
tween M. Thiers and the English Government,
and it is even expected in Paris that Mr.
Gladstone will shortly visit that city.

Assertions that the French Government had
hoensed Public gaming-houses in the diffe-
rent pro viucial towns are categorically denied.

Another vigorous step in vindication of its
rights over the property of ecclesiastical cor-
porations has been taken by the Italian Go-
vernment, and will doubtless cause great
clamour at the Vatican and among the Neri
generally. Part of the house of the Chief
Director of the Jesuits has been occupied de
par le !lei, in order to provide room for the
offices of the military Engineers and the
general staff, transferred from Florence.

According to the return of the Registrar-
Geseral, the mean temperature of the air at
the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, last week
was considerably below the average for the
corresponding period in fifty years; the mean
was equal to 59.2 deg., and showed an average
daily deficiency of 2.9 deg. The temperature
rose considerably on ,„Friday and Saturday,
and on the latter day the mean was 66.5 deg.,
or 5.4 deg. above the average.

Last week 5,362 births and 3,475 deaths
were registered in London and twenty large
cities and towns of the United Kingdom. The
mortality from all causes was at the rate of 25
deaths annually to every 1,000 persons
estimated to be living. In the metropolis
2,408 births and 1,445 deaths were registered,
the former having been 47 above, and, the
latter 147 below, the average number.

The South-Western Railway Company are
importing Belgian coal and mixing it with
Welsh coal in consequenoe of the high price
of the latter. The company's annual con-
sumption is 100,000 tons. A permanent rise
of Os. a ton in the price of coal will make a
difference in the coal expenditure of the
company of £20,000 a year.

Lord Penzance; we are glad to state, has-
considerably improved in health daring the
last few days.

The Prince of Wales has intimated through
Sir William Knollys, his inability to be pre
sent at the laying of the foundation stone
of the new harbour works at St. Helier's,
Jersey. Much disappointment is expressed
at this announcement, as the inhabitants had
made large preparations for the reception of
his Royal Highness.

President Grant is at present residing in
the near neighbourhood of Canada. He is
staying at Pullman Island, one of the Thou-
sand Islands, in the .River St. Lawrence,
closely adjoining the line of division between
the two countries, and about two acres in
extent. He is there the guest of the pro-
prietor, who is better known as the promoter
of the Pullman Car Company.

The death of the Rev. C. W. King, which
took plaoe recently, does not cause a vacancy
among her Majesty's Inspectors of Schools.
Mr. King was on the retired list, and his
piece was filled up some mouths ago.

The Dean of Westminster is so far recovered
from his recent severe illness that he is to
officiate in the parish church of St. Andrew's
next Sunday morning.

Sir Alexander Duff Gordon remains in a
very critical condition.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Lord John
Hay, and Mr. Ponder, M.P. arrived on Tues-
day night at Inverness, in dr. Pender's yacht.
They left the following day fir Dunrobin to
visit the Duke of Sutherland.

The Princess Frederick Charles of Prussia
visited Warwick Castle on Tuesday, and
spent several hours in inspecting that building,
the church, the Beauchamp chapel, and other
objects of interest. The party came direct
from Oxford by an early train, and after the
inspection lunched at the Warwick Arms
Hotel. In the afternoon the Princess left War-
wick station for London en route for.. Ger-
many.

Mr. Barker, one of her Majesty's servants at
Windsor Castle, died suddenly on returning
to his residence on Tuesday night.

The Emperor Napoleon, the Empress
Eugenie, the Prince Imperial, attended by
their suite, arrived at Ryde Pier on Tuesday by
one of the passenger steamers from Portsmouth.
The Empress with her attendants, walked up
the pier, and paid a hasty visit to Brookfield,
the residence of the Marquis of Exeter, his
Majesty and the Prince Imperial meanwhile
sitting and walking on the pier. In a short
time the Empress returned, and the Imperial
party left for Cowes by the steam-packet
amid the cheers of a crowd of spectators.

Prince Arthur has fixed the 19th of Sep-
tember as the day on which he will open
Roundhay-park, which has been recently
purchased by the Corporation as a public park
for the people of Leeds.
•

A handsome monument has been erected in
the yard of the church of St. Miry Tower,
Ipswich, to the memory of the late Bishop of
Melanesia, who was murdered by savages
Sept. 20, 1871.

Arrangements are making by the yacht
builders in the Isle of Wight for building
steam launches of iron. Hitherto none but
wooden steam launches have been built there.

The New York Herald says it is repoTteci
that the complete census returns of the United
States for 1870 give these startling statis-
tics of the population : —Men and boys,
19,493,665 women and girls, 19,064,806;
Surplus of mon and boys, 428,839.

The boatswain and the mate of the brig
Mayflower were proceeding on Wednesday to
their vessel, in a small boat, when it capsized
and they were drowned.

On Friday and Saturday mornings there
were slight falls of snow on Ben Nevis and
the other higher hills in the Lochaher district,
but they melted away after sunrise.

At Portishead the young ladies of Miss
Norman's school went out bathing, and a
governess got out of her depth and was
drowned. The scene is described as very
distressing—the unfortunate deceased strug-
gling for life in the presence of and close to the
pupils, and yet it was impossible to help her.
The body was in the water two hours, and
when picked up life was, of course, extinct.
The deceased, who belonged to London, only
joined the school at Midsummer.

At the Gloucester Assizes on Wednesday, in
an aotion for breach of promise of manage,
" Courtenay v. Stirrup," a verdict was ac-
cepted for £l,OOO damages. The plaintiff is the
daughter of a merchant at Waterford, and
defendant is a gentleman residing at Dilhorne,
Staffordshire.

By Americans it is stated that efforts are
being made at the Court of Arbitration at
Geneva to arrange that the award, which they
consider is certain to be delivered, shall be
made in a fixed gross sum, so as to avoid any
reference to a Board of Assessors.

Two hours' artillery practice from the- cliff
at Trouville wiled away part of M. Thiers's
holiday afternoon—the performance being one
of the best "drawing" for the visitors and
townsfolk. Out of fifty shots from five guns
of different construction and calibre, none hit
the target, moored at 3,000 metres; nor does
any better success seem to have attended the
two consecutive volleys fired from all the
pieces. The Reify° mitrailleuse, pointed by
the designer himself, was then tried, and tired
five times per minute.

At the Old Bailey, on Wednesday, Annie
Wheeler, who had surrendered on an indict-
ment for the manslaughter of an infant child,
was discharged from custody, the grand jury
having thrown out the bill. James Plaster, a.
labourer, was convicted of feloniously wound-
ing one Michael Leary, and was ordered to be
imprisoned for three months.

On Wednesday the two divisions eompris
ing the northern army, as now constituted at
Aldershot, had a field day. Major-General
Lord Mark Kerr's division occupied the ridge
of Fox-hill, the scene of the sensational battle
which formed the concluding incident of last
year's rnancouvres. Major-General Staveley's
division, marching as from Woking to Alton,
attacked the other troops in position, and,
after some interesting fighting, the battle
terminated without a formal decision on the
part of the umpire.

The man Joseph Daniel Rogers, who was
indicted for the murder of his wife at Ber.
mondsey, was tried at the Central Criminal
Court, and acquitted on the ground of insanity.
At the same court Lydia Irenables was con-
victed of the murder of her girl child, three
years old, at Barnsbury, and sentenced to
death. A powerful appeal was made by Mr.
Montagu Williams to hold that, under all the
surrounding circumstances, she was not re-
ponsible for her actions when the deed was
done. Frank Fisher, a hatter, was found
guilty of the murder of Richard Salt, and
sentence deferred. •

A swarm of insects, which were thought
by harvest labourers to be corn bugs, made
their appearance among some men reaping
corn near Brasted, Kent, on Wednesday:
Stings soon convinced the workmen they were
insects of an uncommon character in that
locality, and they made inquiries. The women
and children were the chief victims of these
invaders, which proved to be mosquitoes, an 4
had come from a ship lying oft' Woolwich or
Gravesend.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

Prince Bismarck will assist at the Em-
perors' meeting at Berlin, notwithstanding
that he is not enjoying good health.
The trial of the bishops and priests incul.
pated in Judge Keogh's judgment will take
place in Dublin in January next.

Cholera is increasing in virulence in
Galicia. The epidemic has reached Cracow.
Many oases are reported from the districts of
Doubovel.

Extensive preparations are being made for
the public fetes to be given, at Belgrade, in
honour of the coronation of Prince Milan, and
it is intended by some of the political parties
to impart to the fetes the significance of a
great Solavonian demonstration.

- It is stated that damages to the 'extent of
£14,000 have just been awarded against the
Lyons and Mediterranean Company to eleven
families, members of which were killled or
injured by a train running off the rails at
Champigny on September 16, 1871.
General Sherman left Edinburgh on Tues-
day evening and proceeded to Stirling. In
the course of Wednesday he visited Dundee,
accompanied byl Lord Kinnaird. On arriving
at Dundee Station the deneral was received
by Provost Yeaman. The party drove through
the principal streets, and afterwards visited
the manufacturing works of Messrs. Baxter
Brothers and Co.

The Prince of Wales started in the Duke of
St. Alb Eyes yacht yesterday, on an excursion
to the French coast. His Royal Highness will
first visit Dieppe, and then probably
Trouville and other parts in the Channel.

Thirteen thousand animals are affected with
foot- and-mouth disease in Dorsetshire. Amongst
sheep especially the malady is virulent.
Last Wednesday evening Chelsea was thrown
into a state of excitement by the news that a
double murder had been committed in one of
the numerous disorderly houses in the neigh.
of Cremorne. For the last few days two
young Germans, natives of Berlin, have been
staying at a house in Langton-street. About
nine o'clock on Wednesday evening a woman,
named Elizabeth Curtis, was in one of the
upper rooms of the house and heard a report
of firearms. She ran down and called a
companion, Helen Gordon, who in turn
milled a servant, and the three women went
together into the room from whence the
sound had proceeded. They found lying
upon the sofa a young man dead, and
upon- the floor another one dying. The
landlord of the house at once obtained medi-
cal assistance, when it was found that the
man on thu sofa was shot through the centre
of the heart, and must, of course, have died
instantly. The young man on the floor was
next examined, and was found to be sinking
fast from bannorrhage, and but slight hopes
are entertained of his recovery.
Great excitement has been occasioned in
Fraserburgh, by the arrival of the her-
ring fleet, with a capture higher and more
valuable than has ever before been landed at
that station. Of the 600 boats which entered
the harbour only a few were unsuccessful.
The total will be 12,000 or 13,000 crane, re-
presenting the enormous number of 10,000,000
of herrings, the value of which may be rcundly
stated at .C 16,000 to £16,000.
A curious lawsuit has just been settled in
France. A lady having taken into her mouth
a morsel of the cartilaginous part of a calf's
ear, it went the wrong way and lodged in her
cesophagus. It was extracted by the nearest
doctor, who charged £2O for his services The
lady refused to pay, and said that Dr. Nelaton
himself would not have demanded such a sum.
Dr. Nelaton, on being appealed to by the
medical man, said he considered the charge
moderate. The jury split the difference by
awarding £l2, which it would appear bears a
very small proportion to the costs.

It is officially announced at Paris that tit
Treasury has commenced repaying the surplus
subscriptions to the new loan.

The obstruction caused by the landslip at
the mouth of Peak Forest tunnel having been
removed, the traffic between London and
Manchester has been resumed as usual.

It is stated in a Simla paper that the pension
of Mr. Cowan, of Kooka notoriety, has been
allowed. The Cowan Testimonial Fund now
amounts to 6,318 rupees.

In the Southwark Police-court, Mr. Powell,
an officer of the Coroner of East Surrey, who
is also an undertaker, charged John .Bright
with an assault, and it turned out that the
complainant had put the body of a man, on
whom an inquest had been held, into one of
his own coffins, but afterwards had it transferred
to one belonging to the parish, by which it was
buried. A dispute arose about some property
or the deceased's, which complainant claimed,
and the defendant pushed him out of the
house. The magistrate severely censured
Powell for his conduct, and dismissed the sum-
mons,

THE UNSKILLED LABOURER.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

_
SIR,—Is the unskilled labourer not "a man
and a brother ?" I find in an address to the
Gun Trade Association at Birmingham the
following paragraph
"It has been the fashion to decry trade
societies for taking measures to prevent the
supply of labour (Aceeding the demand by
making restrictions to prevent men finding
their way into a trade who have not earned
their right by a period of probationary servi-
tude, an evil which, if unchecked, reduces the
skilled workman to the condition of the un-
skilled labourer."
Is there not in this sentence involved the
principle of caste? Skilled workmen desire,
like professional men, that their children
should follow, if not their own craft, one of a
like or higher grade. The action of the trades
unions tends to stereotype these castes, and if
not counteracted by other influences would
land us in a condition of society such as we
see in India; the unskilled labourer becoming
the outcast or pariah of society.
Now the BEE-HrvE is "the people's paper;"
1 shall be glad, therefore to see in its columns
some' escape from the evil which seems to me
to be threatening "the greatest good of the
greatest number." •
My own suggestions would be in favour of
freedom of apprenticeship, combined with
organized.emigration.—Yours, ezc.,
(humor.

THE WORKING MAN'S PLA.TFORI.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

_
Sta,—Of course I was much pleased to see
that your correspondent, Lloyd Jones, agrees
cordially with myself in denouncing Mr.
Morley's new political alliance as most unfit
to unite all branches of the Reform party, and
for the, very reasons which I have already
. i given n your columns.
Your correspondent is quite correct in
asserting "That whoever can adjust proper
conditions between the masses of the working
people and the old Reform party (I thank him
for using the word Reform) will perform a
very necessary and a very important work."
Yet, I do not believe that any credit is due to
Mr. Morley for his Cannon-street programme,
because it is self-evident that Mr. Morley's
object. was not that which your correspondent
SO properly commenced, but solely to induce
the working classes to cling to Mr. Cfladstone's
()harlot wheels.
I am old enough to remember, and it is
forty years ago, when the question arose what
should be the nom de plume of the party of
progress. Whig was . pooh-poohed and so
was Liberal, and on these grounds :—1 at.
That any man could call himself Liberal; and,
2nd. That it was unfair and ungentlemanly to
take as a party name that which r really accused
your opponents of illiberality ; and at last
Reformer was almost unanimously accepted,
the principle being that such name was assumed
as that of men who were for progress—pro-
gress, however great or small in quantity
however quicl . or however slow.

For above twenty years this soubriquet was
closely adhered to, but it was too rigid for the
seekers of place, or of title, &n,, and by
degrees the name of Liberal was foisted upon
13.etormers, the great sinner in this respect
being Lord Palmerston, who, himself being
totally destitute of any political principle,
and payed with equal zeal wider the bigoted

Tory and the apathetic Whig of his lordship
and his parasites, it may be truly said that,
if they did nothing else, they so emasculated
the House of Commons, that they made it
possible for a Gladstone to be Premier.
So much for the wide distinetion in principle
which may exist between one calling himself
a Reformer and another calling himself a
Liberal, on which I shall, not say another
word. Mr. Lloyd Jones truly says, A glance
at the Cannon-street programme must satisfy
any thoughtful politician how likely it is to
produce divisions and hostilities. Of course,
but these hostilities and divisions among the
working class will just answer Mr. Gladstone's
views, and secure .Mr. Morley's reward, pre-
cisely the same as though he had obtained
more support from the working class. The
support of the whole, as a class, it would be
impossible for him to obtain, after his con-
ternptuous treatment of them in refusing to
inquire into the expediency of paying off the
National Debt.

Now, if Mr. Gladstone be beaten at the next
general election, the Earl of Derby, if not
Premier, must hold a position in the Cabinet
Of the highest rank, and assuredly, after his
public declaration in favour of the expediency
of paying off the National Debt, he would not
accept such position except upon the distinct
understanding that the expediency of paying
off the National Debt was made the subject of
inquiry by select committee of both Houses of
Parliament, and this it was which Mr. Glad-
stone refused to do.
There is no reason to believe that either
Mr. Disraeli, Marquis of Salisbury, Duke of
Richmond, or any of the recognised leaders of
the Conservative party would be against such
inquiry, and I put it to Mr. Lloyd Jones, as a
thoughtful politician, whether it would be
possible any real friend of the working class
could name any platform which could secure
for them such permanent advantages, and to
such an amount, as the payment of the Na-
tional Debt ?—I am, Sir, your very obedient
servant, , RIGBY WAsoN.
August 20th.

RURAL MESSENGERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SIR,—In your impression of the 10th inst.
appeared a letter from one of a much neglected
class, "A Rural Messenger." I was surprised
at the:mild way in which he stated his ease;
he might, with justice, have struck harder, but
employment under P. M. 0. is a grand school
for the development of," caution."
The above class appear little eared for
either at head-quarters, or with the officials.
conducting "Postal and Telegraph Service"
Associations. I have taken your paper for some
time, and have not seen their grievance stated,
nor their rights advocated; it is continually
London and its various divisional employers
that are dealt with. The P. M. G. says all
letter carriers have fourteen days' holiday. I
have been a " Rural Messenger " some Tears, but
never had a day's holiday given. We have of
late been insulted by the grant of uniform (if
that is uniform which is dissimilat), viz., hat,
Irish coat, texture of bean straw, belt, and an
apology for leggings; trousers we find our-
selves, which breaks the uniformity, no over-
coat, no cape, no provision for cold and wet.
Our wages are low; no advance for length of
service; from home all day ; two homes re-
quired; miry lanes, wet, dirty fields (with
footpaths sadly neglected) to traverse; heavy
loads and long journeys; odd outlying houses
to visit; Christmas boxes a rara avis with the
farming districts ; no promotion except at a
loss in the change of duties. Such are some
of the glorious items of our experiences. Only
think of holding up the above inducements for
a man to join the army of" Rural Messenger"
at the end of his term of enlistment. Please
excuse my tone and length of letter. Insert

wheels passing over his breast dreadfully
